The Opera Coat Is Everywhere—Here’s the Chinese Influence Behind the Trend

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (685 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Elle

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, every item on this page was chosen by an ELLE editor.
  • Recent findings suggest that it’s been living rent-free in my mind for the better part of this year: Conner Ives’s silk brocade opera coat, which captured nearly every fashion lover’s heart when it debuted on the fall/winter 2026 runway at London Fashion Week.
  • The coat—crafted with silk tapestries dating back to the Qing dynasty and with hand-embroidered depictions of red-crowned cranes, bamboo leaves, and flowers—was undoubtedly the first wave in what would become a tsunami of a trend: opera coats.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, every item on this page was chosen by an ELLE editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

Recent findings suggest that it’s been living rent-free in my mind for the better part of this year: Conner Ives’s silk brocade opera coat, which captured nearly every fashion lover’s heart when it debuted on the fall/winter 2026 runway at London Fashion Week. Reminiscent of Mary-Kate Olsen’s fur-trimmed Balmain coat from the 2013 Met Gala, this particular stunner, along with the designer’s other iterations, seems to be what every It girl is wearing.

The coat—crafted with silk tapestries dating back to the Qing dynasty and with hand-embroidered depictions of red-crowned cranes, bamboo leaves, and flowers—was undoubtedly the first wave in what would become a tsunami of a trend: opera coats. And while plenty of faux fur-trimmed coats have made their way onto the market, those featuring Chinese imagery like that on Ives’s iterations have taken center stage.

“There’s been a real change in how people perceive Chinese design,” Cheryl Leung, founder and creative director of Sau Lee, tells ELLE. Leung attributes the opera coat’s rise in popularity to fashion’s shift away from minimalism and consumers’ growing appetite for expressive pieces, richer fabrics, and textures. “Brocade is a great example because it has so much character,” she notes. “The fabrics can be quite ornate, but when you put them into a modern silhouette or style them with something very simple, they feel completely different.”.

Recent findings suggest that chinese design has often been presented through a Western lens, but designers like Leung and Kim Shui are creating work rooted in their own cultural perspectives. Shui, the Chinese-American, Latest York-based creative director behind her eponymous label, has long been drawn to Chinese garments and the ways they communicate identity. “I’m particularly interested in the visual language and craftsmanship of traditional Chinese garments, whether it’s the silhouette of the qipao (a traditional Chinese dress dating back to the Qing dynasty), the richness of brocade, or traditional techniques like embroidery and intricate knot closures,” Shui tells ELLE. “I look at these elements not as things to reproduce literally, but as a vocabulary that I can reinterpret.”.

While the trend has gained widespread popularity, the Chinese design details behind it can sometimes be overlooked. “I’ve seen so many ‘trending winter coat’ videos featuring Chinese brocade coats with fur trim and traditional Chinese embroidered silk coats, but they don’t make any reference to their Chinese origins,” Shui indicates. “Instead of using terms like ‘qipao’ or ‘mandarin collar,’ creators will often describe these details generically as a ‘stand collar’ or ‘high neckline.’ It’s important to acknowledge where these design elements come from and the history behind them—why erase the cultural context?”.

Leung sees the coat’s popularity as an opportunity to bring attention to its history and the designers reinterpreting it. Shui and her team have also been creating content about the histories of brocade, embroidery, and the qipao, as well as the cultural references behind her collections to bring more awareness of the craft to her audience.

“I do think there’s a difference between appreciating a design tradition and overlooking where it came from,” Leung says. “If a designer has been inspired by Chinese textiles, craftsmanship, or traditional clothing, acknowledging that doesn’t take anything away from their creativity. If anything, it gives the work more depth and helps people appreciate the original references.” Shui adds that brands outside the culture have a “responsibility to acknowledge their origins rather than presenting them as an entirely newly introduced aesthetic.”.

Fashion has been both a vehicle for cultural exchange and a product of it—and trends will undoubtedly come and go. Not everyone will be interested in the cultural history of the piece they buy—and Leung doesn’t necessarily think they need to be. Shui is happy to see people from all backgrounds embrace garments from outside of their own cultures. “I hope this renewed interest encourages people to look beyond the garment itself and discover the rich traditions and craftsmanship behind it,” she notes.

Tom Hardy's 5 Most Stylish Characters, Ranked

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (757 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Esquire

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Tom Hardy doesn’t usually play the good guy.
  • Recent findings suggest that that’s partly down to the costume designers, who’ve given Hardy everything from ’60s East End tailoring to Steve McQueen-inspired ’70s outerwear, but it’s also down to Hardy, who has a particular knack for making a wardrobe feel like his own.
  • So, we’ve dug through the archives to rank his best-dressed roles of all time, and one of them’s actually on TV right now.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Tom Hardy doesn’t usually play the good guy. He’s been a forger, a fixer, a getaway driver, a rogue spy, and, in one of his more ambitious films, both halves of the most notorious twins in British crime (not that there’s much competition). Most of them are walking red flags, sure, but they’re red flags in great clothes.

Recent findings suggest that that’s partly down to the costume designers, who’ve given Hardy everything from ’60s East End tailoring to Steve McQueen-inspired ’70s outerwear, but it’s also down to Hardy, who has a particular knack for making a wardrobe feel like his own. Put him in a Western shirt or three-piece and he’ll look equally at home in both (and you’ll want to steal the look, either way).

So, we’ve dug through the archives to rank his best-dressed roles of all time, and one of them’s actually on TV right now. Consider it your new watch list—just ignore the red flags.

Sources indicate that everyone remembers the spinning top and Joseph Gordon-Levitt’s three-piece, but the best-dressed man in Inception is the one who usually gets overlooked: Tom Hardy’s Eames. Costume designer Jeffrey Kurland imagined him as an expat from a Graham Greene novel, and every piece was made from scratch (even though half of it looks straight off a Dries Van Noten runway). Think batik-print shirts, collars spread over relaxed blazers, sharp trousers, and a wallet chain—basically clothes for a guy who spends too long sitting in the sun and definitely doesn’t wear SPF. Then there’s the watch: a gold tank-style antique Kurland picked up from the prop master’s collection—and he’s since forgotten the brand. Reddit’s watch sleuths are still on the case, 16 years and counting.

Legend gave its costume department a very important task: how do you tell Tom Hardy apart from Tom Hardy? Lead designer Caroline Harris and Soho tailor Chris Kerr solved it with buttons: Reggie, the charmer, wears single-breasted suits that feel safe and easy to trust. Ronnie, meanwhile, is the volatile one who gets three-piece double-breasted silhouettes with extra padding to make him look macho. On both sides, though, everything’s cut from vintage fabrics for a lived-in look straight from the hanger. Sixty years on, you could walk into any hotel bar dressed as either and nobody would bat an eye. Until you start talking business, that is.

Recent findings suggest that inspired by the real-world Cold War scandals that rocked British Intelligence, Tinker Tailor Soldier Spy follows the hunt for a Russian mole inside MI6 in 1973. So, as you might expect, it’s lots of men doing stuff in gray suits. Not Hardy’s Ricki Tarr, though. He’s the only agent with any personality, wardrobe-wise, all thanks to costume designer Jacqueline Durran. Her thinking? Steve McQueen on a mission: a shearling coat in Istanbul, a Baracuta Harrington in Paris, and not a standard suit in sight. The kind of menswear every guy on your FYP is wearing today—Hardy was just 15 years early.

Industry observers note that in MobLand, Pierce Brosnan and Helen Mirren head up the Harrigans, an Irish crime family at war on several fronts—and no one knows it better than Hardy. He plays Harry Da Souza, the guy they call when things go wrong, which seems to happen fairly often. Costume designer Rebecca Hale gave him a wardrobe for the job: a battered wax jacket when he’s taking care of the Cotswolds estate, say, or a substantial overcoat when he’s doing business in the city. There’s one exception to the low-key menswear staples, though: his watch. In season one, he wore a solid gold Rolex GMT-Master II, which is reportedly the most valuable watch in the show. Pretty good for the hired help.

Recent findings suggest that mobLand isn’t Hardy’s first Guy Ritchie gangster part. In RocknRolla, he’s Handsome Bob, the Wild Bunch’s getaway driver. And while everyone else looks like they’d had someone ‘”taken care of” before lunch, Hardy’s low-key menswear staples make him look more like the boy next door. A faded denim shirt. A classic bomber with jeans. A blue checked Western shirt, open just far enough. All simple pieces that let his charm do its thing, which it does when he sweet-talks a lawyer into revealing who’s been grassing to the police. Four years earlier, he played Clarkie in Layer Cake, another member of a London crime crew but one with a very different wardrobe: slicked hair, blazers, open shirts, brandy, and cigars. Similar JD, just with a very different wardrobe.

Olivia Colman debuted a sophisticated hair transformation Monday night at the premiere of Only Murders in London.

Celebrating the sixth season of the Disney+ show, in which she guest-stars alongside Steve Martin and Selena Gomez, Colman wore head-to-toe Celine, walking the red carpet in a striking silk cape top, tailored trousers, and pointed boots.

It has been revealed that equally elegant was the Oscar-winning actress’s upcoming hair color, her second in as many months. Earlier this autumn, Colman debuted a polished “smoky steel” hue; however, she stepped out in the capital this week with an inky black shade.

Hairstylist Earl Simms created Colman’s upcoming look, and the actress joins a handful of other celebrities embracing dark, moody tones this winter. This month alone, Dakota Johnson was seen sporting fresh, jet-black hair, while Billie Piper and Hailey Bieber have also gone considerably darker in recent weeks.

As the nights draw in and summer becomes but a distant memory, many stylish women opt for deep, cozy hues at salon appointments, and while dark brunette shades are generally lower maintenance than bright blondes, there are still a few housekeeping rules, as Luci Green, a colorist at London salon Larry King Hair, previously told Bazaar.

Recent findings suggest that while brunettes might need less frequent touch-ups than blondes, any chemically colored hair still needs care and attention. “The best way to treat freshly coloured hair at home is to always use a professional color protect shampoo and conditioner,” Green explained. “It’s also important to avoid using too much heat,” she added.

According to recent reports, but first things first: Always get a consultation. Green shared: “I’d always advise having a consultation with a colorist before any color change, so they can work out what the best shade is for your skin tone.” Noted!

💡 Key Takeaways
  • If there’s one Apple product line where the recent price hikes hit the hardest, it’s the MacBook.
  • Industry observers note that as luck would have it, Black Friday deals on Apple tech have landed on Amazon, with up to 20 percent off MacBooks—including the brand-new M6 MacBook Pros on sale for the first time ever.
  • It has been revealed that of course, not all MacBooks were created equal.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If there’s one Apple product line where the recent price hikes hit the hardest, it’s the MacBook. Rising RAM and storage costs have pushed laptop prices up across the board, which makes scoring a newly introduced MacBook on sale all the more mission critical.

Industry observers note that as luck would have it, Black Friday deals on Apple tech have landed on Amazon, with up to 20 percent off MacBooks—including the brand-new M6 MacBook Pros on sale for the first time ever. Given that these prices have reached record highs lately, these discounts are certainly nothing to sneeze at. In fact, now that the MacBook pricing status quo has been reset, we’d say this is probably as low as MacBook prices will get these days.

It has been revealed that of course, not all MacBooks were created equal. While the standard MacBook Air is great for most, those who are planning on running hardcore software might benefit from a beefed-up MacBook Pro. And if budget is your primary concern, we’re of the opinion that the MacBook Neo is a worthy buy, even if it’s only $50 off right now.

Sources indicate that the best MacBook Air deal you’ll find right now is this $300 discount on the 15-inch model. With this laptop, you’ll get Apple’s M5 chip in a fanless, 3.3-pound frame that handles heavy multitasking and light video editing without breaking a sweat. Base storage doubled to 512 GB this year—a great upgrade for storing more apps, photos, and files—and the 15.3-inch Liquid Retina display is sharp and vivid. You also get a 12 MP Center Stage camera that’s great on video calls, Wi-Fi 7 for fast downloads, and up to 18 hours of battery, enough for a busy workday and then some.

If you’d prefer a smaller laptop, 13-inch models are up to 19 percent off. They’ve got everything the 15-inch models have, just in a more portable package. The rule of thumb for choosing between a Pro and an Air? The slimmer Air won’t replace a MacBook Pro for serious creative work or gaming, but for school, business, and general use, it’s the one to get.

Apple 2026 MacBook Air 13-inch (M5, 16 GB RAM, 512 GB).

Apple 2026 MacBook Air 13-Inch (M5, 16 GB RAM, 1 TB).

Apple 2026 MacBook Air 15-inch (M5, 16 GB RAM, 1 TB).

Sources indicate that given that Apple just dropped a new slate of M6 MacBook Pros, in addition to the company’s first-ever touchscreen laptop, we were anticipating discounts on the old range of M5 models to clear out inventory. Sure, the best MacBook Pro deal you’ll find right now is $250 off the 14-inch M5 model—but, if you don’t mind paying just $50 more, you can scoop up the shiny new M6 on sale, complete with improved speed and boosted AI capabilities. It’s extremely rare for Apple to discount its latest laptop so soon after release, and even more rare for it to be $200 off.

Both the M5 and M6 models feature Liquid Retina XDR displays, up to 24 hours of battery, three Thunderbolt 4 ports, HDMI, an SD card slot, and up to 2 TB of storage.

Sources indicate that why go Pro over the Air? The GPU is fast, which makes a difference when editing video, working with high-res photos, or gaming, and the XDR screen is significantly brighter. If your daily workload has started becoming too much for the Air to handle, this is where you should look next. If you want the biggest, most powerful model possible, souped-up MacBook Pros with more RAM are up to $500 off.

Apple 2025 MacBook Pro 14-Inch (M5 Pro, 16 GB RAM, 1 TB).

Apple 2025 MacBook Pro 14-Inch (M5 Pro, 24 GB RAM, 1 TB).

Apple 2025 MacBook Pro 16-Inch (M5 Max, 36 GB RAM, 2 TB).

Recent findings suggest that the MacBook Neo is Apple’s most affordable laptop, even with the recent price hike from $599 to $699. Right now, the Neo is $50 off, sitting smack in the middle between its debut price and post-increase price, at $649—making it far and away the cheapest MacBook.

Industry observers note that the Neo is an easy recommendation for anyone looking for their first Mac. It runs on Apple’s A18 Pro chip and is surprisingly quick for browsing, sending email, and streaming video. The 13-inch Liquid Retina display looks great for the price, and the battery lasts a solid 16 hours. It also comes in four fun colors, with the yellow-green citrus being a fan favorite.

There are some trade-offs with going with Apple’s budget model, including storage that starts at 256 GB, just 8 GB of RAM, and no keyboard backlight. You also get only two USB-C ports, so getting a USB-C hub is a must if you proposal to connect a lot of accessories. Spending an extra $100 gets you a Neo with 512 GB of storage and a Touch ID sensor for quick unlocking. For students or anyone who mostly sends emails and browses the Web, the Neo is hard to beat.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I’ve been writing gift guides as a shopping editor for years. Usually, I’m very sentimental, wanting to recommend thoughtful gifts to make your loved ones smile. But all bets are off when it comes to White Elephant gifts. I want to cause chaos at your family gift swap. Your gift should be the one everyone fights over.

If you're not sure what a White Elephant exchange is or how it works, just know this: it's really fun, and it's one of the only times when stealing is not only totally acceptable, but encouraged. Basically, it's a blind gift exchange that, when the recipient reveals the gift they chose, they can keep it or put it back and steal someone else's gift. It's a cheeky little game that is a great way to get into the holiday spirit.

It’s also a really affordable way to exchange gifts as a substantial group. No worries about finding the perfect thing for someone specific. Just bring something cool enough for anybody to enjoy, and there’s usually a budget cap. So for this guide, I provided the best white elephant gifts under $50. They’re so budget-friendly and unique that you might want to do all of your gift shopping below, or buy some items of your own. Worry not; we won’t judge.

Additional copy by Jessica Cherner.

This is the ultimate tool for any candle lover. In just one sleek, swan-shaped package, it’s a candle snuffer, wick dipper, trimmer, and wax spoon. It comes in gold or raven black, and it’ll be perfect coffee table decor.

No city-dweller will say no to extra storage. It’s especially helpful when it comes in a cute and colorful package, like these cache boxes. Use it to hide junk mail, Q-tips, or any other tiny clutter.

Sources indicate that the plant lover in your life will jump at the chance to steal this care essential. Yes, they might own a wine opener already, but we doubt it’s as cute as this corkscrew. The color-blocked bow tie shape makes opening the next bottle look even more fun. A bar cart isn’t complete without it.

Industry observers note that if you love pickles, you’ll understand why this one won’t last long in the White Elephant pile. No more digging into the jar to grab the perfect spear. This mini-fork makes every charcuterie board way easier to assemble.

Industry observers note that the commuters in the room might argue over this one. Anyone who meal-preps will love this portable food warmer. Keep your lunch nice and toasty, whether you have a microwave within reach or not. Plus, it’s spill-proof and dishwasher-safe.

We all have days that feel extra difficult to deal with. And this deck of affirmations is tongue-in-cheek, but motivational enough to get through it. “I keep this on my desk for the longest workdays,” McKenzie says. “100 little reassurances to make me laugh.”.

Latest Update: How Nara Smith Crafted Her Style From Scratch

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish

💡 Key Takeaways
  • The Good Buy is a podcast from Harper’s Bazaar in which editors Leah Chernikoff and Lynette Nylander invite celebrities, designers, models, and tastemakers to talk shop: what they buy, where they got it, and why it matters.
  • Industry observers note that it’s been three years since Nara Smith first burst onto the scene, carving out her own niche of CookTok with her highly stylized “from scratch” videos, in which she makes home-cooked versions of everyday food for her family.
  • Sources indicate that smith has translated this signature formula into brand deals and partnerships, “cooking” Marc Jacobs totes and sunscreen bottles from scratch.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Good Buy is a podcast from Harper’s Bazaar in which editors Leah Chernikoff and Lynette Nylander invite celebrities, designers, models, and tastemakers to talk shop: what they buy, where they got it, and why it matters. Come down the fashion rabbit hole and take a peek inside the closets and shopping carts of the world’s most stylish people. Learn how they use style to tell their stories.

Industry observers note that it’s been three years since Nara Smith first burst onto the scene, carving out her own niche of CookTok with her highly stylized “from scratch” videos, in which she makes home-cooked versions of everyday food for her family. Narrating her process in a soft ASMR voice, she’s crafted everything from Skittles and Starbursts to chili soup and cornbread, with easy-to-follow (yet labor-intensive) recipes now immortalized in her debut cookbook, Homemade. Always dolled up and dressed in an archival ensemble or a look pulled straight off the runway, she’s blurred the lines between food and fashion—and managed to make spending a full day in the kitchen look utterly glamorous.

Sources indicate that smith has translated this signature formula into brand deals and partnerships, “cooking” Marc Jacobs totes and sunscreen bottles from scratch. She’s sat front row at Fashion Week, embarked on a cookbook press tour dressed in Schiaparelli vegetable prints, and starred in Skims campaigns alongside her model husband, Lucky Blue.

It has been revealed that she’s a chef, a writer, a model, and a mother—but if there’s one title she wholeheartedly rejects, it’s that of a trad wife. “That’s one of the narratives that I have a really hard time wrapping my head around,” she told Harper’s Bazaar. “You don’t see me getting on a plane, hopping to New York, modeling, coming back—all while I have a newborn—paying bills, filming content, getting my kids dressed. Being put into a certain box, just because people think that I’m slaving away, is so weird to me. I’m a working mom who gets to go about her day in a very different way than [someone with] a normal nine-to-five job would.”.

“I love dressing up. I love fashion so much,” she continued. “Sometimes my outfits aren’t the most practical, but then again fashion isn’t always practical. That’s what I do. I post videos of me cooking for my kids and my husband. It’s really not that deep.”.

Now, the star joins Harper’s Bazaar’s The Good Buy to dive into where she shops, the designers catching her eye, and how she styles herself for video shoots.

In a recent development, “It’s my Super Bowl. It’s so fun seeing what brands send down the runway, it’s nice to see trends, it’s nice to see what everyone’s gravitating towards—but it’s also so nice catching up with friends. I’m always like, ‘I don’t know anyone,’ but then I go and I’m like, ‘Hello, hello, let me say hi to that person.’ It’s always really fun, and then I get to dress up. I’m a glam girl, fashion girl, through and through.”.

“It was [an IMG Models contest.] I hash-tagged all of my photos and then one day [scout] Jeni Rose reached out to me via DM. And two weeks later, I was in Paris. I don’t know why they stated ‘That girl.’ My eyebrows were so thin, I was in the highest heels you could imagine, couldn’t walk in them. I was 14. And they saw something in me that I didn’t at the time.”.

Sources indicate that “I met my husband and I moved to the States and I couldn’t work because of my visa situation. In that time, we also had two kids. So I was like, ‘Okay, I’ll stay at home with them, you go model.’ So Lucky did what he did, and after a while, I was finding my way back into modeling while also simultaneously starting to post on Instagram and TikTok. I got diagnosed with an autoimmune [disorder] which forced me to cook, and then without knowing I really just blew up and then transitioned into a content creator.

“It’s nice having built a name that is a brand, to where now I get to collaborate with brands. It’s not just me being a model or a mannequin for a brand, where I’m bringing their vision to life. Now it’s a collaboration, because they usually tap into what I have to offer and it feels like I have creative control and I can speak my mind. It feels very warm.”.

It has been revealed that “I forget [how major the audience is] because to me, it’s my phone and me in the kitchen with my tripod. I don’t have a team, I don’t have people at my house. It’s me styling myself, getting myself ready, doing the recipes, doing all of these things. And then I post it and I go about my day. But then when I leave the house and I get stopped a bunch, I’m like, ‘Oh! People actually watch me.’ And I get so excited.”.

Recent findings suggest that “I think about where my counter cuts me, which is around my hips, so I make sure everything hip and up is good. Sometimes the bottom is a little wonky or I’m not wearing a shoe. I feel like tops can get boring, so I try to play with silhouettes and textures or sleeves.

Recent findings suggest that “Sometimes I like to match the color or the texture [to the food]. Sometimes I like to match the time period. I remember I made a milkshake and I was like, ‘When were they really popular? What were they wearing in that era?’ There’s always some element that ties it back to what I’m making.”.

It has been revealed that “It was a Bottega bag, a big brown woven one. That was my first splurge ever, and I felt sick to my stomach about it for three weeks. I thought about returning it for so long, but I’m glad I didn’t because it fits everything.”.

“I don’t think I regret buying anything, because I’m really careful. If it’s not an immediate yes, I will leave the store and think about it for weeks. I remember this vintage Cartier watch that I saw two years ago and I still think about it daily. Maybe in a few years I’m going to get it, but it was just too much money to spend. Maybe when I hit 30.”.

Recent findings suggest that “Vintage denim. You can never have enough denim. They come in all washes, all sizes, all cuts—I love a bootcut, I love a flair, I love a straight cut. The possibilities are endless. I have been really lucky where I walk into stores and they look at me and pull me stuff. Ebay is great. Or my husband—sometimes I’ll go onto his side of the closet and I’ll get a pair and take it to the tailor. He’s never gonna know.”.

According to recent reports, “There’s this Schiaparelli jacket that just walked down the runway; it has vegetables on it. They gave it to me for this press tour, but I want to buy it when it comes out and it’s probably going to cost me an arm and a leg. It feels special. It feels like it’s in my realm. The craftsmanship is insanity, and the color black is so velvety and saturated, it pulls you in. And it fits me like a glove.

In a recent development, “If I do splurge, I want it to be timeless enough. If [my daughter] Rumble sees that in 30 years, she’s going to think that’s the most iconic jacket she will ever see. When there’s an estate sale, when I’ve passed? Do you know how iconic that’s gonna be?”.

Industry observers note that “I got some Sonny Angels that were really cute—these little figurines with cute heads. Also, my friend Iris [Law], she’s the most whimsical person. We never get time in Paris, but we got time in Paris, and she knows the best [shops]. She took me to this perfume place with the best Parisian perfume that has all these stories. So I kind of went ham and bought a bunch of perfumes. And one of them was a scent that Marilyn Monroe wore.”.

Sources indicate that every item on this page was chosen by an ELLE editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

There was a time when satin seemed reserved for summer evenings or special occasions, but that has changed. Nowadays, the silky fabric is being paired with richer textures for everyday fall and winter outfits, not just for parties.

It all comes down to styling, and it’s a lesson in contrasts. Fall and winter are all about texture, so teaming a satin skirt with a soft cashmere knit keeps the look sleek and sophisticated while bringing a cozier feel to daytime. For evening events, silk on silk is a natural choice, and you can always add a faux-fur scarf or stole to embrace the cold-weather spirit.

According to recent reports, color plays its part, too. Swap summer’s pastels for deeper, moodier shades such as chocolate brown, bottle green, burgundy, and navy, which lend satin a richer, more seasonal feel. Champagne and ivory remain timeless, especially when worn head to toe beneath a tonal wool coat.

Whether you’re dressing for a holiday party, a workday, or a weekend brunch, below we’ve rounded up some inspo for how to style satin this season.

We love the contrast of silky, sheer balloon pants with a sporty neoprene jacket. Finished with Tabi ballet flats, a woven tote, and sleek sunglasses, the look feels effortlessly chic, even on a day of errands.

In a recent development, DONNI. The Silk Cotton Sheer Balloon Pant.

Maison Margiela Tabi split-toe leather ballet flats.

Denmark’s Queen Mary is looking posh and joyful on day two of her historic state visit to Colombia—a trip which makes her the first Danish queen to travel to the country.

Today, the monarch was given a tour of the Gold Museum in Bogotá, and later walked through the city’s main square, Plaza de Bolívar, with Mayor Carlos Fernando Galán.

The official visit runs through November 26, and the queen’s agenda includes learning about the country’s post-earthquake reconstruction efforts (three months after a 7.4-magnitude earthquake struck Colombia) and ongoing sustainability projects.

To arrive in the country, Mary went sharp in a black Forte Forte single-breasted blazer with a frilly sky-blue Stenströms Darya blouse, which she paired with black trousers, Malone Souliers Marion 70 pumps, and black Gucci glasses, plus some gold jewelry.

Then, for this afternoon’s engagements, she slipped into a sophisticated business look, the highlight of which was a black-and-white tweed pencil skirt from Dolce & Gabbana and a black collared top from Red Valentino. To round out the ensemble, she reached for sheer black tights, plus matching stilettos and a leather handbag.

The royal performed another quick change for her evening engagement: a reception in the Biodiversario greenhouse at Bogotá’s Botanical Garden. The look was a breezy wine midi dress with a fun dotted print by Saloni. In semi-sheer fabric, it featured a high neck, long sleeves, a cinched waist, and a long skirt that reached her ankles. Black-and-white heels added the perfect contrast to the colorful maxi.

The Best Pregnancy-Safe Sunscreens, According to a Dermatologist

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (724 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Elle

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that every item on this page was chosen by an ELLE editor.
  • Sources indicate that pregnancy often requires an overhaul of your skin care routine—mainly due to ingredients not being tested for safety during pregnancy and because hormonal shifts can cause skin changes that require a upcoming set of products.
  • During pregnancy, Olamiju recommends mineral-based sunscreens as the first choice.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that every item on this page was chosen by an ELLE editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

Sources indicate that pregnancy often requires an overhaul of your skin care routine—mainly due to ingredients not being tested for safety during pregnancy and because hormonal shifts can cause skin changes that require a upcoming set of products. One non-negotiable in any daily skin care line is sunscreen. Although the choice between chemical SPF and a mineral one is usually a personal preference, several considerations should be made during pregnancy, under the guidance of a medical professional. Dr. Brianna Olamiju, a board-certified dermatologist with Spring Street Dermatology in NYC, explains to ELLE which are the safest sunscreen formulas to use during pregnancy and which ingredients to avoid.

During pregnancy, Olamiju recommends mineral-based sunscreens as the first choice. Look for formulations with zinc oxide, titanium dioxide, or a combination of both. “Mineral sunscreens work by forming a protective layer on the skin and are particularly appealing during pregnancy because their active ingredients have minimal absorption through the skin,” she explains. They also tend to be well tolerated by individuals with sensitive skin, which can become more reactive during pregnancy.

Some of Olamiju’s top picks are EltaMD UV Physical Broad-Spectrum SPF 41, La Roche-Posay Anthelios Mineral Tinted Sunscreen SPF 50, CeraVe Hydrating Mineral Sunscreen SPF 50, and Blue Lizard Sensitive Mineral Sunscreen SPF 50. “For patients experiencing melasma or pregnancy-related hyperpigmentation, I particularly like tinted mineral sunscreens containing iron oxides, as these provide additional protection against visible light, which can contribute to worsening pigmentation,” claims Olamiju. Ultimately, she adds, the best sunscreen is one that feels comfortable on the skin and that you’ll want to use consistently.

Industry observers note that according to Olamiju, there’s right now limited research specifically evaluating the safety of chemical sunscreen ingredients during pregnancy. However, she notes this does not mean all chemical sunscreens have been proven unsafe. “Some chemical sunscreen ingredients can be absorbed through the skin and detected in the bloodstream, but systemic absorption alone does not establish that an ingredient causes harm to a developing baby,” she explains. At this time, there is insufficient evidence to conclude that using chemical sunscreen as directed causes adverse pregnancy outcomes.

Recent findings suggest that that noted, as a precautionary approach, she recommends choosing mineral-based sunscreens containing zinc oxide and titanium dioxide during pregnancy. “It is key to emphasize that patients should not avoid sunscreen altogether out of concern about chemical ingredients, as protecting the skin from ultraviolet radiation remains extremely important during pregnancy.”.

Recent findings suggest that the sun protection factor (SPF) is important during pregnancy, just as it is any other time. Olamiju explains that pregnancy can increase the likelihood of developing hyperpigmentation, particularly melasma, commonly referred to as the pregnancy mask. “Hormonal changes can stimulate melanin production, making the skin more susceptible to discoloration, especially with sun exposure.” To get ahead of it, she recommends using a broad-spectrum sunscreen with an SPF of at least 30, although she adds that an SPF 50 is an excellent option for those who spend significant time outdoors or are particularly prone to pigmentation.

Recent findings suggest that as a precaution, Olamiju recommends avoiding sunscreen formulations containing oxybenzone and octinoxate when practical, given research concerns raised about their potential endocrine-disrupting properties and the limited pregnancy-specific safety data. Beyond sunscreen filters, she says to also be mindful of other active ingredients like retinoids, including retinol, tretinoin, and adapalene, which should be avoided during pregnancy, as should hydroquinone. “When in doubt, patients should review their skincare regimen with their dermatologist and obstetrician.”.

It has been revealed that in addition to a mineral-based formula with zinc oxide, titanium dioxide, or both, and an SPF of 30 or higher, Olamiju also recommends a water-resistant sunscreen, particularly if you exercise outdoors, swim, or spend extended periods in the sun. For anyone experiencing melasma or increased pigmentation during pregnancy, she also indicates to consider a tinted mineral sunscreen containing iron oxides to provide additional protection against visible light. If you have sensitive or pregnancy-related reactive skin, you may also benefit from fragrance-free, noncomedogenic formulations. “I generally prefer lotions, creams, or sunscreen sticks over sprays to ensure adequate application and minimize the risk of inhaling airborne particles,” Olamiju adds.

This Forgotten ’90s Comedy Is the Most Demented Thanksgiving Movie Ever

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1760 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Esquire

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Let’s start off by acknowledging that the late John Hughes wrote and directed the greatest of all Thanksgiving movies with Planes, Trains and Automobiles.
  • This road-trip saga that Hughes penned and produced in 1991 is by the numbers in most ways but excels in its brazen wrongness, even by the free-range standards of Generation X.
  • Hughes didn’t direct this one, handing off those duties to Peter Faiman, who had worked extensively in Australian TV and only made one other feature film: 1986’s Crocodile Dundee.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Let’s start off by acknowledging that the late John Hughes wrote and directed the greatest of all Thanksgiving movies with Planes, Trains and Automobiles. There are definitely other great ones, but … Dutch is a different kind of creature. This is a Thanksgiving family comedy in which a grown man fights, kidnaps, and abandons a child. Occasionally he holds him at gunpoint. It’s a rotten child but a kid nonetheless. The movie still made me laugh, but it was mostly in disbelief.

This road-trip saga that Hughes penned and produced in 1991 is by the numbers in most ways but excels in its brazen wrongness, even by the free-range standards of Generation X. I come here to praise this messy movie, not to bury it. It’s a relic from when films could be wilder, shaggier, and more shocking than the rigidly tame family comedies of today. Dutch is many things, but it is not refined to baby-food levels of inoffensive smoothness.

Hughes didn’t direct this one, handing off those duties to Peter Faiman, who had worked extensively in Australian TV and only made one other feature film: 1986’s Crocodile Dundee. I can’t help but feel this was an experiment gone wrong, or maybe a first draft that needed another pass from Hughes. It’s built out of leftovers from better road-trip movies, and like any Frankenstein’s monster, this one runs straight into a wall and ultimately falls apart.

But if you want something different for your Thanksgiving watch, go find this one. Fair warning: It’s not streaming anywhere in the United States, so you’ll have to seek it out on a sketchy Russian bootleg site that makes it look like the footage was ripped from a worn-down VHS.

According to recent reports, dutch stars Ed O’Neill as the title character, a blue-collar guy sent to pick up his girlfriend’s blue-blooded son from a Georgia boarding school and deliver him to Chicago in time for the holiday feast. The not-so-surprising catch is that the kid (played by a 13-year-old Ethan Embry) mercilessly despises Dutch, and honestly the feeling is mutual.

Doyle is one of the most hateful kids in comedy history. Even the ginger demon of Problem Child was more cartoonishly mischievous than sociopathic. Embry, who was then credited as Ethan Randall, isn’t playing a troublemaking scamp like the kid in O. Henry’s “The Ransom of Red Chief” or Hughes’s own Home Alone. He’s a smug sociopath with a violent mean streak.

Industry observers note that we learn that Dutch is a salt-of-the-earth cousin to O’Neill’s uncouth Al Bundy from Married with Children because he flicks the caviar off his cracker at a fancy party. (“I make it a rule never to eat anything a fish deposits in a riverbed.”) Okay, fair.

Compare that to how we meet Doyle: Another young boy in his boarding school comes to his room to say he has a call on the dormitory’s community phone line. “Someone from any sort of decent background would knock,” Embry’s character hisses. He then corrects the kid’s vocabulary and threatens to report him to the school administrators for mild cursing. So he’s a snob, a prick, and a rat. But even this is within the bounds of film comedy. You could picture an older version of him as a stuck-up villain in Caddyshack or Animal House.

Industry observers note that then there’s another, even more disturbing phone scene when Doyle gets the bad news that his rich father won’t be helping him get out of this road trip with Dutch. He hangs up and stalks past an elderly janitor who is sweeping the hallway, silently kicking over the garbage can to scatter trash across the helpless old man’s feet. There’s no joke. He’s just a son of a bitch.

Doyle would fit in great with the Children of the Corn, except he’d scowl at their shabby farm clothes.

It has been revealed that obviously this kid is going to get some form of comeuppance. When Dutch demonstrates up at his dorm room to start the trip, Doyle beats him with a golf club and shoots him in the testicles with a BB gun. Something about this is much more violent and visceral than the Looney Tunes–style pratfalls and clobberings of Home Alone.

According to recent reports, they have a fistfight in the tiny room, and Dutch seizes the weapon. Does he toss it away or break it? No—he uses it himself to hold the kid at gunpoint. We have just crossed beyond the boundaries of comedy, never to return. Dutch then ties the boy up, lashes him to a hockey stick for easier carrying, and stuffs underwear in his mouth to muffle his cries.

You know a movie is going off the rails when watching it makes you feel like you should be testifying against the characters as a witness for the prosecution.

In a recent development, so begins the drive, with Dutch and Doyle doing their best to annoy each other verbally. Then comes a bizarre scene in which Dutch stops for fireworks for some reason and sets them off in a snowy field while the kid watches from the car. I suppose he’s trying to inspire a little playfulness in the boy, but it just seems like Dutch has lost it and is indulging a pyromaniac streak.

In a recent development, it goes wrong and he sets his coat on fire, which makes it harder to understand why he loses his temper when the boy flicks the butt of his lit cigar at him. The man just went mano a mano with a whizzing fireworks spinner, but this is what lights his fuse?

Dutch does the reasonable thing. He abandons the boy in the snowy night and tells him to walk the rest of the way to the motel. “About 50 miles down the road!” Fifty miles? Okay, Dutch, I believe we’ve added another felony to the charges.

This isn’t one of those moments where the grown-up pulls over just beyond the tree line and waits for him. Dutch actually goes to the hotel, although he occasionally puts down his paperback and checks the window to see if the boy has made it there alive. When Doyle finally does show up, shivering and wet, Dutch claims, “Here’s something you should know about me. I don’t fool around. You piss me off, I react.”.

Uncle Buck certainly had its off-color and irresponsible moments, but even that havoc-prone babysitter might have called Child Protective Services over this situation.

Sources indicate that doyle responds by stealing Dutch’s car keys while he sleeps and parking the sedan sideways in the snowy road, where it is slammed into by an 18-wheeler. This is a comedy, so the hapless truck driver is not killed on impact.

Recent findings suggest that faiman shoots all of this with too much gritty realism. Maybe it would work if it was all a little zanier and over the top (think of Vacation), but Dutch just plays less like a series of set pieces and more like an array of crime scenes. They don’t call anyone for help because Dutch doesn’t want to admit to his girlfriend how badly things are going, so they hitchhike the rest of the way and stay in a homeless shelter, where the rotten kid learns that a lot of people have it much worse than he does.

In a recent development, at one point, they are picked up by a pair of pretty young women who are driving home from a job at the Superdome in Fresh Orleans. “We’re call girls,” one of them explains. Hoo boy. Here we go.

It has been revealed that but thankfully—mercifully—Dutch goes no further than showing the kid sleeping in the backseat with his head resting on the chest of one of the women. Not great, but it could be worse. (Worse is when Dutch tries to bond with the child over a deck of naked playing cards.).

In a recent development, even Dutch seems to recognize that “prostitute road trip” probably isn’t the ideal situation for a young boy. But he explains it in the most vulgar way possible: “You and I are riding in the backseat from now on, because what that missile twister can teach you, you don’t need to learn until you’re in prison.” Then the ladies drive off without them, taking Dutch’s wallet and leaving the pair stranded again.

In a recent development, they spend the next leg of their trip riding in the open concrete pipes in the back of a long-haul truck, but they fall asleep and wake up in a trailer depot where they are roughed up by two security guards. Doyle responds by drawing his BB gun on them and making them believe he is going to blow their heads off.

Recent findings suggest that this same joke was deployed by Chevy Chase in the Hughes-scripted National Lampoon’s Vacation (“Are you kidding, this is a Magnum P.I.”) but here, again, it just plays as psychotic violence rather than absurd humor. “The kid is crazy,” Dutch tells the men as they beg for their lives.

Recent findings suggest that by the time the duo finally get home for the Thanksgiving meal, the hostility between Dutch and the kid has softened into a grudging respect. I know: Surprise! Back at the mother’s house, Dutch physically assaults the boy’s callous father, leaving a mark with his pinkie ring on the jerk’s forehead. Instead of an assault charge, it all ends happily ever after with a callback to an earlier gag: Dutch pulls the BB pistol from his pocket and indicates it’s time to get the revenge he promised he would one day seek. As the boy’s smile fades, Dutch aims the gun at him—and us (!!!)—as the film cuts to the credits.

Oh, Dutch … you dangerously inappropriate maniac. Don’t ever change. And, well, he doesn’t, although the kid goes through the expected metamorphosis to become a more sensitive and understanding human.

It has been revealed that they don’t make ’em like this anymore, as the saying goes, and I actually think that’s a pity. Dutch isn’t all that funny, but neither is toothless humor that’s overly safe. I’d gladly tolerate a few misfires like this if it meant more truly unhinged comedies like we had in the ’80s, ’90s, and early 2000s. Dutch stands as a throwback to when small-scale comedies weren’t afraid to take big swings—even if they occasionally landed against someone’s skull or testicles.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Every item on this page was hand-picked by a House Beautiful editor.
  • Pictured above: A refreshing sunroom with built-in bookshelves by Doniphan Moore.
  • While embracing home design trends can be fun for a while, it can get really old really quickly.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Every item on this page was hand-picked by a House Beautiful editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

Pictured above: A refreshing sunroom with built-in bookshelves by Doniphan Moore.

While embracing home design trends can be fun for a while, it can get really old really quickly. Of course, if you really like something, then by all means, decorate your home with it. However, if you’re simply reaching for the things that are popular at a current moment in time before throwing them out after you realize you don’t actually like them, then it might be time to invest in some more timeless decor.

It has been revealed that “Ultimately, timeless design is all about creating spaces that are beautiful, functional, and meaningful,” notes Abby Pendergrast, an interior stylist and set designer. “That’s why people are drawn to these classics—they make a house feel like a home, and that never goes out of style.”.

Ahead, we asked a handful of designers to share the pieces and choices they deem timeless. From gilded mirrors to striped textiles, keep reading to see the 10 things that designers promise you’ll love for years to come.

Additional copy by Meghan Shouse.

Antique chests and dressers will never go out of style because they’re well made piece that only get better with time.

Recent findings suggest that “They were meant to last for many years, acting as heirloom pieces for generations to come,” says Debbie Mathews LeRoy of Debbie Mathews Antiques & Designs. They’re multifunctional to use as storage or a spare surface, and they can easily move from room to room and house to house.

According to recent reports, “An antique chest brings history and warmth to any space,” designer Emily Jiles of Maggie Griffin Design explains. “Mixing in an antique chest gives the room a collected feel and adds character that newly introduced furniture often can't replicate.”.

It has been revealed that golden mirrors add a touch of elegance to any room, and they’re shockingly versatile. They can bring more luxury to a traditional style home, or they can add a historic air to a more modern space. Mathews LeRoy, however, specifically adores Louis Philippe giltwood mirrors.

Industry observers note that “It can live happily in a traditional interior or fit within a transitional interior thanks to its simple arched shape with minimal decoration,” she indicates. “They boast understated elegance and can be beautiful in an entrance hall or foyer, dining room, living room, powder room, or bedroom!”.

Industry observers note that like any classic choice, bookshelves will grow with you as your sensibility evolves and changes. They can be endlessly re-styled and adjusted to hold whatever pieces you acquire along the way. Plus, they are a kind of diary of the books you are reading and the conversations you are having.

“Literature never goes out of style. A home without books isn’t a home in my opinion. And a bookshelf acts as a blank canvas to explore your innate curatorial abilities,” says Alex Bass, founder and CEO of Art Advisory & Interior Design Studio Salon 21. “It is also something that grows with you and that you can constantly reorganize. So investing in a good one with timeless appeal is key.”.

High-quality natural materials such as wood or stone just get better with time. “Using natural materials in your home is always a good idea,” claims Pendergrast. “They bring warmth, texture, and that feeling of authenticity we all crave.”.

Wood, whether it’s flooring, furniture, or even ceiling beams, adds a cozy, lived-in vibe, while stone is durable and elegant. “Wood and stone age gracefully, developing character as the years go by. They’re versatile enough to fit into any style, from modern to rustic, which means you won’t have to worry about them ever going out of fashion,” she states.

While we're on the topic of natural materials, let's not forget this inimitable combination. Marble and wood both have a knack for adding character and aging beautifully, and they're not just for kitchens. Think: Wooden chairs pulled up to a marble-topped dining table or a wood coffee table or console with a marble top. The combination is “both timeless, modern, and neutral while bringing a luxurious feel to your space,” indicates Bass.

Industry observers note that leather furniture carries memories—as a piece ages, its patina changes. And a leather chair can hold its own—the material has weight and personality that make it an excellent companion to a wide range of nearby colors, fabrics, and patterns. “It fits any type of design aesthetic, whether you’re going for something more mid-century or more traditional,” Bass notes. “I love seeing the wear in a piece, the cracks and the wrinkles.”.

Sticking with paint colors inspired by nature—such as soft blues, calming greens, whites, and warm tans—helps create a peaceful and balanced space. “These colors are easy on the eyes and make your home feel more like a retreat,” Pendergrast says. “Earthy, natural shades are always in style because they have this effortless way of grounding a space. They act like neutrals, so you can easily switch up your decor over the years without having to repaint the whole place.”.

A wooden table, such as an antique farm table, is a timeless piece worth investing in. As demonstrated in this space designed by Clara Jung of Banner Day Interiors, it grounds the room, allowing other decor choices to be light and airy. Whether it’s a coffee table, side table, or made for a dining room, “You’ll always find use for it and it’s something sturdy that will never go out of style,” Bass states.

Stripes are a classic pattern that doesn’t ever feel too trendy. “You can throw them on curtains, rugs, or even wallpaper, and they’ll add a bit of structure without overpowering the room,” Pendergrast states. “Whether you go bold or keep it subtle, stripes always find a way to fit in.” The best part about stripes is how flexible they are. “They work with just about any style, and because they’re so simple, they won’t clash with other patterns or elements in your space,” she adds.

In a recent development, built-in details such as crown molding or wainscoting give your space instant character. Your home may already have these features, but if it doesn’t, they are often simple additions you can implement. “These features add a little polish without feeling too stuffy, and they make the room feel more custom and unique,” Pendergrast notes. “Crown molding and wainscoting have been around for ages, and they’re not going anywhere.” These architectural details are subtle ways to add depth and elegance to a room. Even better is that they can blend with any style, whether your vibe is traditional or modern.

The new series takes place 80 years after that original film. What’s changed? Who’s in charge now? Before you press play on Blade Runner 2099, let’s run through the cast and characters.

This is the official description of the series from Prime Video:.

Which of the latest characters are human? Which ones are replicants? Does it even matter anymore? Here’s what you need to know.

Olwen is an old-school replicant Blade Runner on the verge of retirement.

According to recent reports, michelle Yeoh is a former pageant queen, ballet dancer, and Academy Award-winning actress. You know her from Everything Everywhere All At Once, Wicked, Crazy Rich Asians, Memoirs of a Geisha, Shang-Chi and the Legend of the Ten Rings, Star Trek: Discovery, American Born Chinese, and Crouching Tiger, Hidden Dragon. She is also a Golden Globe, Critics Choice, and Actor Award winner. Before all of that, she had a prolific Hong Kong action and martial arts filmography. Legend!

Cora is a replicant who goes undercover as a human.

Bebeto is a human who teams up with Cora.

Elias is Cora’s younger brother.

He played a young version of Peter Capaldi’s character in the Black Mirror episode “Plaything.” His film credits include gnarly horror movies like The Severed Sun and The Damned. Next you’ll see him in the ensemble cast of Lorna Tucker’s Bare.

Yahya is another replicant Blade Runner.

Matthew is best known for playing Larys Strong on House of the Dragon. (His co-star Freddie Fox also appears in the Blade Runner 2099 pilot.) He also played Lucien Bonaparte in Ridley Scott’s film Napoleon, and starred in the medical drama series Casualty. Some of his television credits include Jerico, The Hour, and classic literary adaptations like War & Peace, Great Expectations, and The Musketeers. You’ll see him next in Robert Eggers’ Werwulf and the upcoming Elden Ring movie.

Amy Lennox is a prolific West End theater actress who was nominated for an Olivier Award in 2016. She played Chloe Godard on 100 episodes of the medical drama Holby City and also starred in the short-lived sitcom Only Child.

Katelyn Rose Downey plays Greta.

This St. Bart’s House Was Designed to Look Nothing Like Its Neighbors

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1070 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Elledecor

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Few clients ask their designer to make the bedrooms in their vacation home smaller and simpler, but that was just the edit the homeowners made to prepares for their house in St.
  • According to recent reports, situated on a steep hillside above one of St.
  • A Caribbean island is a challenging place to work under any circumstances.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Few clients ask their designer to make the bedrooms in their vacation home smaller and simpler, but that was just the edit the homeowners made to prepares for their house in St. Bart’s, indicates designer David Ries. “They didn’t want these humongous bedrooms with huge floating beds and massive bathrooms.” Instead, the couple wanted to be able to host as many people as possible, a request that didn’t surprise Ries, who’d already worked with the family on homes in Manhattan, Long Island, and Telluride. “It’s what this client has always asked for. They can’t have enough bedrooms.”.

According to recent reports, situated on a steep hillside above one of St. Bart’s famously pristine white sand beaches, the house had initially been a boutique hotel. The blueprint was to turn it into a retreat for themselves and their adult children and grandchildren. The family are longtime visitors to the island—“the daughter told me it was her ‘happy place,’” indicates Ries, lead designer of the New York-based interior design firm Ries Hayes—and knew exactly what they wanted. Not the white box look popular with luxury new builds on the island, but instead something reminiscent of the “old St. Bart’s,” says East Hampton-based landscape designer Edwina von Gal, who, like Ries, has collaborated with the clients on other projects.

A Caribbean island is a challenging place to work under any circumstances. Everything has to be brought in from far away, including all the plants, which came by barge from Miami. St. Bart’s in particular requires anyone building to work with a local architect and engineer. In their initial proposal, this French team defaulted to that “slick and modernist” look, as von Gal describes it, with the oversized bedrooms and white color scheme that dominates much of the island’s luxury housing stock.

Industry observers note that the design team pushed back—asking for a lot of bedrooms (eight) and generous living spaces. They also had strong opinions on the building materials. Given the island’s climate, the humid, salt-soaked air can be hard on everything. “If we did white paint, which is prominent throughout St. Bart's, it’s constant maintenance, constant painting,” says Ries. The design team insisted on cladding the buildings in Ipe, the durable tropical hardwood, which wears well. It mystified the local architects and set the complex apart from its neighbors. It also makes the buildings disappear into the greenery of the hillside.

Sources indicate that but the architects rapidly caught on to the latest plans, and von Gal is eager to praise their technical accomplishments. Regulations require properties to conserve rainwater, so there are cisterns beneath the buildings, plus technology infrastructure and laundry facilities. “Working on the hill is so complex,” she notes. “It's such a tight little package of technology and function. What they did was amazing.”.

Industry observers note that the team decided to reconfigure the property as a series of pavilions that face the view of the ocean and surrounding hills. The main entry is at the top of the steep hill, along with parking. The next level down is for family bedrooms; below that is a primary suite and study; and finally the fourth level is the main living space, including a playroom. “We made sure this playroom was front and center,” says Ries. “My client loves her grandkids.”.

The playroom and study have built-in daybeds that can be used as spare guest rooms in a pinch. But the clients did get their eight bedrooms. “We know how to make compact bedrooms and make them very efficient, make them very livable, which allows us to fit in a lot of space for a lot of guests, and then that puts a lot of emphasis on having main entertaining spaces that are big and gracious,” says Ries. “The idea is that everybody hangs out together.”.

According to recent reports, everything is united by generous outdoor spaces, which wind between the bedrooms. “Every room has an amazing view,” says Ries. “It feels almost like your own little treehouse in a way.” The bottom living area opens out to a pool and an expansive deck where the family eats most of their meals.

The house has an elevator, but stairs are the primary way the family moves between levels and finally down to the beach. “We hung on for a really great, gracious, fun set of stairs,” notes von Gal. “They really introduce you to how amazing the different levels are and all the wonderful secret places.”.

Durable fabrics and materials were chosen throughout and Ries made sure everything could be easily moved around and reconfigured. Outside on the main deck, three long dining tables from Sutherland were outfitted with casters so they could be maneuvered into a single long table or several smaller ones; 26 lightweight dining chairs can be pulled from different parts of the deck. If the infamous “Christmas winds” bring a downpour, the tables can even be moved indoors so a dinner party can proceed in inclement weather. Outdoor seating can be arranged as a 15-foot sofa or several love seats.

Sources indicate that “It's so flexible,” says Ries. “We know this from working with a client that their needs for entertaining change every day, or sometimes a couple times a day.”.

Industry observers note that the kitchen is also efficient, designed to produce easy, clean meals. The family would rather spend time in the pool than over a stove. And no part of the living room is oriented around a TV. “They're readers,” says Ries. “There’s always stacks of new books when you go to their homes. So there’s all these cool little spots you can tuck into.”.

Sources indicate that ultimately, the client and design team’s insistence on what they wanted paid off—but it wasn’t without a few moments of doubt. “When so many people are telling you ‘no, surely this is not what you want,’ it does start to erode your confidence a little,” claims von Gal. “Then when it does come out well, there’s a real sense of triumph and satisfaction.”.

In a recent development, tour this St. Bart’s Family Home.

A fresh coat of paint is one of the easiest ways to give your home a little refresh before the holidays, but you don't necessarily have to take on an entire redesign project to make an impact.

It has been revealed that some of the most interesting places to introduce color are the details you might normally overlook. They're relatively small surfaces, but a little paint can make them feel like intentional design features, adding character and definition without the time, expense, or commitment of repainting every wall.

Whether you want to make a statement, add a little contrast, or create a more interesting backdrop, there are plenty of ways to make a big visual impact with a relatively small project. Ahead, designers share the unexpected spots worth painting before the holidays and how to choose colors that feel right at home.

It has been revealed that window casings are an easy detail to overlook, especially when they're painted the same white as the walls and trim throughout the house. But introducing a little color around the windows “can emphasize the proportions of a window and give the room more definition,” says designer Sarah Cole. Even if you're not ready to go bold, she adds that “a subtle contrast can make a difference.”.

For a more traditional look, Kristen Thomas of Ink & Canvas Design recommends pulling from a historical or traditional palette, pointing out that “colored trim was once a sign of status in early American homes” because rich pigments were costly and difficult to come by.

When time is tight before the holidays, this simple painting project can be achieved in a single afternoon. Just don’t forget the painter’s tape.

In a recent development, don't overlook the design impact of the interior doors in your home—a hallway lined with plain white doors can feel a little forgettable, but painting one or two in a contrasting shade can give the space a more intentional look. Paint it early enough, and you may be able to hang a wreath from it.

Sources indicate that massimo Buster Minale, founder and creative director of Buster + Punch, believes an accent like this “can completely shift the character of a room.” And you don't necessarily need to choose a bright or dramatic color to get that effect. Picking one you love, rather than going all-in on a trendy shade, is key.

It has been revealed that “I recommend choosing a grounding color and adding some whimsy with the small touches,” indicates Lee Crowder, National Director of Design and Model Experience at Taylor Morrison. Before painting, take a look at the doors in adjoining rooms so you can decide whether a single standout door or a more consistent color story makes the most sense.

If you have built-in bookshelves or cabinetry, you already have a natural spot for a little color. Rather than repainting the entire unit, try painting just the back panels. This also gives you the opportunity to declutter what’s already there. Cole recommends this pre-holiday spot because “it adds depth and helps books and collections stand out.” Her advice for choosing a shade? “Pull a color from the room's upholstery, rug or artwork.”.

Industry observers note that thomas also recommends painting built-in shelving and cabinetry as a way to create a special feature in the room. “Painting built-ins sets them apart as a special feature and creates a beautiful backdrop for your favorite objects and holiday decor,” she indicates.

Instead of going for a bold contrasting hue, Vivian Robins at Arketa Design Studio suggests using a color that already appears elsewhere in the space, explaining that this small paint enhancement can work as a “punctuation mark” in the room.

“Sometimes the smallest design changes create the biggest impression within a room because you're drawing out a color that lives in the space,” Robins adds.

Blade Runner 2099 Is a Beautiful Slog Through a Grim Future

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (644 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Esquire

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Flying cars darting through smog and neon skyscrapers.
  • Streaming now on Prime Video (and just in time for a long holiday weekend) is Blade Runner 2099.
  • Hunter Schafer flexes some of her budding leading-lady chops as Cora, a real human posing as a Replicant to smuggle herself and her brother out of Los Angeles.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Crowded streets. Long, cool coats. Flying cars darting through smog and neon skyscrapers. An abundance of Japanese aesthetics that imply America’s lost superpower status. Ridley Scott’s seminal 1982 masterwork Blade Runner (itself adapted from Philip K. Dick’s Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep?) laid the foundation for almost all of cyberpunk science fiction, so much so that everything else feels undeservedly derivative. Even a new Blade Runner. The new series Blade Runner 2099 looks the part, but it lacks the soul of its predecessors, leaving its perspectives on what it means to be more human than human hollow, like a Replicant without memories of its own.

Streaming now on Prime Video (and just in time for a long holiday weekend) is Blade Runner 2099. A stand-alone continuation of both Ridley Scott’s towering original and Denis Villeneuve’s remarkable legacy sequel, the series takes place in 2099 (decades after Villeneuve’s Blade Runner 2049). An unseen revolution has elevated Replicants to the ruling class of Los Angeles, rendering flesh-and-bone meat-bag humans as the new discriminated minority.

Hunter Schafer flexes some of her budding leading-lady chops as Cora, a real human posing as a Replicant to smuggle herself and her brother out of Los Angeles. Her ruse leads her to Olwen (Oscar-winner Michelle Yeoh), a Replicant Blade Runner spending the final days of her artificial life span seeking out someone from her past. A humorless buddy-cop mystery, Blade Runner 2099 is mired in a plot-centric narrative that cares less about the why of all things—an underrated and beautiful feature of its predecessors—than the what and how.

In other words, it’s the first time a piece of Blade Runner media actually zeroes in on the plot, instead of anything else more interesting. Try not to think of this as an eight-hour Blade Runner series but rather an eight-hour series stretching at the seams to feel worthy of its branded title.

Is it because streaming TV in 2026 has become so plastic and hollow that even Blade Runner 2099 feels like an unengaging slog? Or were the direction of both Scott and Villeneuve so immaculate that we were distracted from how turgid they might have been all this time? Regardless, 2099’s lack of auteurship is its most deafening shortcoming. The series has been steered to the screen by executive producer Silka Luisa, whose warmer color palettes—based on her choice of more sunshine, which glistens off surfaces—lend 2099 some identity. Some.

But beyond even that minor distinction, Blade Runner 2099 is still just a plot-y crime drama that checks off boxes and goes through the motions of its genre, with nary a real thing to say. About us, about our fragile humanity, about the demise of all we’ve built through artificial intelligence. Blade Runner 2099 is a dystopian sci-fi in all the ways you expect it, but it’s hardly a good one. Sure, the original movies were oppressive, dreary, and morbid too. But they possessed a knowing glare into our fears about the future and our imminent collapse as a civilized species. The new series lacks this same insight, or indeed any of its own, all in the name of goosing up engagement numbers for the closest thing to a real-life Tyrell Corp. (Do shareholders dream of electric quarterly reports?).

Industry observers note that despite surface-level similarities to the movies, plus a moody noir-like motif with a sexy saxophone that, admittedly, completely and unapologetically rips, the plodding Blade Runner 2099 is a needless walkabout through a world that never begged for one. Needless is a good word, actually. The show’s strong visual execution is negated by its inability to rise to the occasion as a worthwhile or enlightening probe of the human experience, or even just as an entertaining cop show. It may be smart, but what good is intelligence if there isn’t an ounce of grace?

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Founded as a seaport more than 350 years ago, Charleston evolved into one of the most important trade hubs in colonial America. As the South Carolina city’s wealth grew, handsome estates began filling up its coastline. But throughout Charleston’s rich, colorful, and complicated history, the city never had a high-end hotel that took full advantage of its waterfront setting—until this year, with the debut of The Cooper.

Located on the site of the former State Ports Authority headquarters (which was demolished in 2019), the 191-key property sits on Charleston’s historic peninsula and overlooks the Cooper River. Interiors by Champalimaud Design pay homage to the city’s maritime heritage, referencing the “Lowcountry” culture that took root in the surrounding region.

Sources indicate that “We wanted The Cooper to feel like a natural extension of the city, balancing the ease of a waterfront home with the refinement of a luxury hotel,” indicates Jun Chun, principal at Champalimaud Design. “The overall inspiration was Charleston itself, particularly its coastal heritage, architectural history, and gracious, unhurried way of life.”.

It has been revealed that the six-story property, which is operated by Beemok Hospitality Collection, has a relaxed feel infused with a subtle Southern flavor. The experience starts before guests even step inside thanks to an entryway lined with an allée of crepe myrtle trees—a Charleston staple with tumbles of showy, hot-pink blooms.

Inside, the lobby sports creamy marble flooring with a basketweave pattern that nods to the local art of braiding sweetgrass. Meanwhile, a mural inspired by changing tides lines the spiral staircase, leading to the public areas upstairs.

The hotel’s Mediterranean-style signature restaurant, The Crossing, helmed by chef Nick Dugan, was designed by multidisciplinary studio Meyer Davis. (There are three additional, smaller dining venues on site.) For the restaurant’s meandering floor plan, the design team created a series of distinct indoor and outdoor spaces, hewing to a marshland palette of soothing neutrals and calming blues as well as strategic doses of lacquer, teak, and honey onyx.

References to the local culture continue in the guest rooms, which feature bespoke headboards, wardrobes, and credenzas adorned with woven details, once again tying back to vernacular craft. “We approached the guest rooms as elegant waterfront homes rather than traditional hotel rooms,” notes Chun. “Wide-plank oak floors, painted shiplap walls, woven textures, and residential-style Roman shades establish a sense of warmth and familiarity.”.

Among the amenities are a 7,000-square-foot spa as well as a heated saltwater infinity-edge pool on the fourth-floor terrace. The pool deck, which has its own bar, overlooks not just the harbor but even more perks: a latest waterfront park by Rees Roberts + Partners plus a private marina, where guests can charter one of the property’s cruising vessels, such as a Hinckley motor yacht.

For the design team, bringing The Cooper to life was a careful balance of respecting tradition while also looking forward. “Charleston has an extraordinary architectural heritage and a strong tradition of craftsmanship, and we wanted to acknowledge those qualities without simply reproducing the past,” explains Chun.

“Ultimately, we wanted The Cooper to feel as though it belongs in Charleston today and will continue to feel relevant for years to come.”.

Industry observers note that geoffrey Montes is an associate editor at ELLE Decor with a serious love for all things real estate and design. Before that, he worked at Architectural Digest, Galerie, and Preservation magazines, covering everything from jaw-dropping listings to world-famous architects and design events like Salone del Mobile and Homo Faber.
