It has been revealed that now, this is the part where you take it all in, rewatch one (or four) of your favorites, decide what you agree with, what you simply cannot stand for, and let us know about it. Let’s walk through the tunnel together, shall we? These are the best fifty sports movies of all time.—Brady Langmann.

Burt Reynolds stars in The Longest Yard as the incarcerated former quarterback, Paul "Wrecking" Crewe, who was kicked out of the NFL after admitting to point shaving. While in prison, he convinces the football-obsessed warden to let the inmates play a game of football against the guards, even though the seemingly harmless activity only exacerbates the power dynamic between them. But unlike most underdog sports stories, The Longest Yard’s setting pushes themes of reclaiming your self-worth in the face of a cruel, authoritarian system much more than its competition. —Josh Rosenberg.

Recent findings suggest that the Pride of the Yankees arguably did more for the legacy of its star, Gary Cooper, than its subject, baseball legend Lou Gehrig, but it was 1942 for goodness’ sake. The film was rushed into production and premiered in theaters just a little over a year after the Newly introduced York Yankees player died from a rare disease that would later be named after him. And if it wasn’t for Cooper’s incredibly earnest portrayal, the conventional biopic likely wouldn’t have had the same effect—even with recency bias and Babe Ruth playing himself. But twenty bucks says you can’t watch Cooper give Gehrig’s real-life farewell speech at the end of the film without shedding a tear. —J.R.

The first time the Fast & Furious franchise swerved from street races and highway heists came in the standalone 2006 sequel, Tokyo Drift—the first helmed by Fast Saga mainstay Justin Lin. Set in the world of Japanese drift racing (originated by motorcyclist Kunimitsu Takahashi and mastered by “Drift King” Keiichi Tsuchiya), troubled American teenager Sean (Lucas Black) moves to Japan to live with his father, where he gets caught up in the motorsport’s resurgent scene. Basically The Karate Kid on wheels, The Fast & the Furious: Tokyo Drift is about the only time these movies proved it didn’t need Vin Diesel and barbecues to be a thrill. —Eric Francisco.

We know what you’re thinking: Clint Eastwood’s Million Dollar Baby exists. But allow us to make a case for his 2009 drama Invictus. Set in 1995, after apartheid, Invictus demonstrates how the Springboks national rugby team—led by Francois Pienaar, played by Matt Damon—united South Africa through their victory (spoilers?) at the 1995 Rugby World Cup. One of their biggest motivators was Nelson Mandela (Morgan Freeman), whose democratically elected presidency was equally symbolic of South Africa’s journey to reconciliation. Where Million Dollar Baby was a deeply personal (and harrowing) tale of one woman in the boxing ring, Invictus is about an entire nation in desperate need of something to believe in. —E.F.

The Major Lebowski is a bowling movie. You might not think about that right away, especially since the Joel and Ethan Coen comedy starring Jeff Bridges starts with a California slacker who’s simply on the search for his missing rug. But amid all the crime capers and accidental kidnapping plots, the heart of The Big Lebowski is a film about a group of guys—including John Goodman and Steve Buscemi, a.k.a. the dream blunt-rotation bowling team—who just want to take down rival bowler Jesus Quintana (John Turturro). If Hollywood ever makes a traditional bowling movie as good as The Big Lebowski, you can bet that it will still be compared to The Dude every step of the way. —J.R.

How many sports movies actually created a team? Only The Mighty Ducks. In the original that started it all, Emilio Estevez stars as a hotshot lawyer whose community service leads him to coach a ragtag youth hockey team. During his state-mandated service, he rediscovers his lost love for the ice. There have been sequels and even a two-season Disney+ revival series—and Disney’s brief ownership of a real franchise, the Anaheim Ducks, who won the Stanley Cup in 2007—but the first movie is still undefeated. Ducks Never Say Die! —E.F.

In 2011, the MMA business was booming. Tickets were through the roof, the UFC was finding its place on primetime, and fresh leagues like ONE Championship took off. So it was a good time for Gavin O’Connor to unleash his smashing drama, Warrior. Tom Hardy and Joel Edgerton play two estranged brothers whose entry in a mixed martial arts tournament forces them to confront their fractured relationship. Warrior hits hardest where it counts, and functions as an early showcase of Tom Hardy’s brawny charisma. —E.F.

I’m not one of those sickos who wishes that rollerball was a real sport, but that doesn’t mean I don’t enjoy watching it. Especially when, in the dystopian world of the fictitious sport—which combines roller derby, handball, biking, and outright bloodthirst—James Caan is the GOAT. The ‘70s cult classic earns its spot in our rankings not because of the rollerball action (which is thrillingly directed by Norman Jewison), or its retro-futuristic set design, but because of its prescient vision of a sports league that is shrouded in rich, manipulative C-suiters and a controlling body that, well, only wants to control. —B.L.

Nobody respects the referee. And why should they? They’re always slowing down the game and making terrible calls. I mean, are they blind, dumb, or both, you know what I’m saying? Well, when fanatical baseball fan (and umpire hater) Bill Johnson (William Bendix) is forced to go to umpire school after losing his job in this silly 1950s comedy, we all learn a thing or two about why the game actually needs an impartial bystander who keeps the game clean. Even if he can’t seem to see the damn ball. —J.R.

Is the John Huston movie where Sylvester Stallone and Michael Caine play POWs at a German camp who form a soccer team, play said Nazis in soccer, and escape at the end of the game extremely cheesy? Yes, it absolutely is. But is it ... also sort of amazing to watch Stallone earnestly play goalie, Caine direct his squad like a seasoned Premier League manager, and Pelé—yes, Pelé is in this film—deke up some Bambi-legged Nazis? Also yes. I won’t spoil the method in which Pelé scores a goal, but it’s so stupidly fun that it solidified Victory’s place on this list. —B.L.

In a recent development, want a sports-movie take that has earned me some flak around the Esquire office? Of the two Ron Shelton-directed, Kevin Costner-starring sports movies—Tin Cup and Bull Durham, of course—I much prefer Tin Cup. The golf comedy has it all: a perfectly sleazy Costner performance, the sly intellectualism of Bull Durham, a pitch-perfect Tex-Mex backdrop, a Cheech Marin-played caddy, and, most importantly, a Jim Nantz cameo. Its premise, which sees a problematic ex-pro take another shot at the PGA Tour, has more influence than you’d think; look no further than Owen Wilson’s Apple TV comedy Stick, which plays like a loving homage to Tin Cup, right down to the shaggy Winnebago. —B.L.

It has been revealed that dodgeball is, without question, one of the stupidest movies ever made. Even among the Anchormans and American Pies of the late nineties/early 2000s, this sports comedy starring Vince Vaughn and Ben Stiller about a group of average Joes who compete in a dodgeball tournament to save their gym from being taken over by a fat-shaming, corporate fitness giant has no business being packed to the gills with so many memorably hilarious lines. I wish we had a hundred more movies where Stiller is the antagonist, because his fitness freak White Goodman is one of the funniest villains of all time. Dodgeball even inspired ESPN to actually air bizarre sports on its fictional spinoff channel ESPN 8 “The Ocho,” and I can’t say any other sports comedies ever had that much of an impact on the real world. —J.R.

When I saw The Way Back, which stars Ben Affleck as a struggling alcoholic who is asked to return to his high school to coach its basketball team, I immediately felt like it was one of the greatest sports movies ever made. That was at a press screening in March 2020—you can see where I’m going with this. The pandemic washed out what should’ve been a genuine moment for Affleck and the film, because The Way Back is a stunning character portrait with one of the boldest endings in all of sports cinema. I said this to its writer, Task creator Brad Ingelsby, around this time last year. “I think it's one of the best performances Ben's ever given,” Ingelsby told me. “I really believe that.” That makes two of us. —B.L.

Sources indicate that breaking Away might just be the most underappreciated film on this list. How underappreciated? Well, all three of us hadn’t seen it until longtime Esquire research editor Kevin McDonnell alerted us to its greatness. And damn, was he right. On the surface, Breaking Away is a classic midwestern coming-of-age dramedy: Four teenagers (played by Dennis Christopher, Dennis Quaid, Daniel Stern, and Jackie Earle Haley) clumsily figure out post-high-school life amidst the class wars of Bloomington, Indiana. But Breaking Away’s Oscar-winning screenplay—which layers a climactic cycling competition on top of it all—is so damn smart, funny, and full of teenage heartache that you’ll wish Hollywood made more like it nowadays. Or, at the very least, more high-stakes biking movies. —B.L.

Sources indicate that after The Wolf of Wall Street and Suicide Squad, Margot Robbie became Hollywood’s new it girl. But her Oscar-nominated performance as controversial skater Tonya Harding in the 2017 crime biopic I, Tonya, cemented her prestige status. The movie is based on the life of Harding, her contentious relationship with her mother (played by Allison Janney), and her connections to the infamous 1994 assault on rival Nancy Kerrigan. Robbie pulls out all the stops for a 10/10/10 performance, with an extreme focus on ice skating as a tougher, dirtier sport than the bedazzled outfits imply. —E.F.

Sources indicate that cool Runnings isn’t just a joke. As funny as a Jamaican bobsleigh team is—and was when the real-life team debuted at the 1988 Winter Olympics—Canadian actor John Candy (Planes, Trains and Automobiles) wouldn’t star in a comedy film in the nineties coaching a ridiculous sports team unless it also had some heart. Luckily, Cool Runnings has loads of it. The good-natured comedy for the whole family was a smash crowd pleaser. It took the focus off the Olympics’ superhuman competitors and proved that anything was attainable with the right camaraderie. —J.R.

Mention the Von Erichs to anyone of a certain age from Texas, and they’ll tell you how vital they were to the community—and how cursed they might have all been. Based on true events, Sean Durkin’s musclebound tragedy follows the rise and demise of the Texas wrestling dynasty, the Von Erichs. As the owners and stars of World Class Championship Wrestling, the Von Erichs were on their way to immortality until a series of events tore them apart. Though The Iron Claw is packed with body slams and sweat, its story about the strength of brotherhood in the face of tyrannical masculinity makes it a transcendent tear-jerker. —E.F.

Sources indicate that it’s to be expected for sports movies to be about dirty, dehydrated athletes. But only Bring It On dared to fix its cameras on the cheerleaders. An early 2000s classic and a cable TV staple, the movie follows the rivalry between an affluent suburban cheerleading team (led by Kirsten Dunst) and an inner-city Los Angeles squad (led by Gabrielle Union). After Dunst’s character learns her team’s dynamite routine was stolen from the East Compton Clovers, she works to come up with a newly introduced idea from scratch before a national competition. Don’t let the high-pitched cheers and pearly white teeth fool you; Bring It On is an honest-to-goodness examination of cultural appropriation and the class and cultural divisions even amongst American youth. —E.F.

It has been revealed that timothée Chalamet, who has a debilitating fear of heights, stood atop the Las Vegas Sphere to promote Marty Supreme. While the man went home from the Oscars without a statue, he still left behind one of the best, unlikeliest sports movies in recent memory. Set in 1952, Marty Supreme stars Chalamet as an ambitious hustler with a silver tongue (and orange balls) who is dead set on serving as America’s emissary in the most exciting sport of the postwar era: ping pong. Essentially Uncut Gems in pleated pants, Marty Supreme isn’t actually about table tennis, but about the hustle, and whether it’s in your favor or not, you have to respect it. —E.F.

I’m a sucker for Rounders. The 1998 indie gem starring a cooler-than-all-of-us Matt Damon and a peaking Ed Norton as poker sharks is still a brilliant watch. And I’d be remiss if I didn’t mention the ace up Rounders’s sleeve: A terrifying villain in John Malkovich’s Teddy KGB (the name still gets me), who you genuinely believe would drain the life savings of a guy like Damon’s Mike McDermott and not give a single shit about it. Give Rounders a watch today, and it’s hard not to feel how visionary it was in showing how young men’s lives are hooked, warped, and ruined by the allure of gambling. Remake Rounders today and McDermott might just have DraftKings and FanDuel as the most-used apps on his phone. —B.L.

Sources indicate that the Karate Kid is one of the main reasons why I took up martial arts as a child (along with Power Rangers), and I imagine it was much the same for most nineties kids. Not just because Daniel LaRusso (Ralph Macchio) and Rocky director John G. Avildsen replicated Stallone’s underdog magic for teenagers, but because the film helped create one of the best spiritual mentors of all time in the late Pat Morita’s Mr. Miyagi. There are few training methods as iconic as “wax on, wax off” and few villainous aims more menacing than “sweep the leg, Johnny.” But if you master the former, and avoid the latter, you just might learn what martial arts are really about. —J.R.

It has been revealed that how Warner Bros. ever convinced basketball phenom Michael Jordan to star in this half-animated/half-live-action Looney Tunes basketball movie is beyond me. Because, if I’m Michael Jordan, you show me any storyboard frame from this film during pre-production and I’m bolting for the door faster than the Road Runner. But I’m beyond grateful that the basketball GOAT saw the vision behind Space Jam, because it’s unbelievable how this film wasn’t just an achievement in animation but also one of the greatest sports movies of all time. Really think about that for a second. One of the most celebrated, family-friendly sports movies of all time stars Michael Jordan and Bugs Bunny. Who could have seen that coming? —J.R.

Kumite! Kumite! Kumite! The movie that cemented Jean-Claude Van Damme’s status as the coolest ass-kicker of the 1980s, Bloodsport is still a good time even if it can’t shed its beefcake cheese. It is based on the very tall tales (read: bullshit) of Frank Dux, who claimed to be a U.S. Marine and ninjutsu master who won a secret underground tournament in Hong Kong. Whatever. Bloodsport still rocks as an exhibition of JCVD at his prime. It is The Karate Kid for dudes cracking open mini-fridge beers, and it’s awesome. Fun fact: The original Mortal Kombat started out as a pitch for a Van Damme arcade game due to the success of Bloodsport. —E.F.

There are plenty of movies like Slap Shot in the sports-movie oeuvre: a great athlete, nearing the end of his time in the game, undergoes an existential crisis that somehow turns into one last great winning run. It’s just that Paul Newman did it best in Slap Shot. The 1977 comedy, which follows a mess of a hockey team that turns to outright violence to win games and boost fan interest (however morbid) is still an absolute blast to watch, especially when those damn Hanson brothers drop their gloves. Heated Rivalry could never! —B.L.

In a recent development, the WNBA was in its infancy when Gina Prince-Bythewood’s Love & Basketball hit the court. Sanaa Lathan stars as Monica, a girl with hoop dreams who grows up next door to Quincy (Omar Epps), the son of an NBA baller. As they grow up as childhood best friends before becoming lovers in college, Monica and Quincy eventually learn to square their relationship with their professional aspirations. In most sports movies, romance is a subplot for the main character. Here, love is the very name of the game. And it’s a slam dunk. —E.F.

You can think of Major League as a funnier, better Ted Lasso set in the world of professional baseball (and the Hannah Waddingham analogue an actual villain). Tom Berenger, Charlie Sheen, Wesley Snipes, and more fill out the roster of the Cleveland Indians. After a vindictive new owner (Margaret Whitton) buys the team and prepares a move to Miami, the players spend their final season dramatically improving their game just out of spite. Everything comes down to a climactic division playoff game against the one and only New York Yankees. It’s a cliché to call Major League a “home run” or whatever, so instead I’ll just say it has nice velocity. —E.F.

In my book, The Hustler is the greater billiards film over its legacy sequel, The Color of Money. (Sadly, I was overruled.) Sure, the latter has Tom Cruise. But the original black-and-white Paul Newman film better captures the stress of betting on pool, swathed in the smoke of cigars and just the right blood-alcohol level to concentrate without second-guessing yourself. Throw in George C. Scott as a professional gambler and Jackie Gleason as pool shark Minnesota Fats, and you have one of the most star-studded and high-stakes films of the sixties—all over the act of poking some billiard balls into table pockets. —J.R.

Sources indicate that never before has tennis been so exhilarating—and, we’ll say it, titillating. Luca Guadagnino’s meme machine of 2024, Challengers, raised the bar as an erotic sports drama about two former best friends (Josh O’Connor and Mike Faist) torn apart over a beautiful tennis ace (Zendaya). During their tense reunion at a rinky-dink tournament, they compete to settle things once and for all. Between Guadagnino’s dizzying camera and the dynamic duo of Trent Reznor and Atticus Ross going beast mode on the soundtrack, Challengers had us all spending one summer bringing our situationships to the theater. It was a weird summer, admittedly. —E.F.

Industry observers note that who can forget the Beast, or Wendy Peffercorn, or those long summer nights playing ball under glittering fireworks? The Sandlot is the ultimate love letter to adolescent, Americana-flavored nostalgia, where boyhood friendships are forged in the cauldron of baseball. Set in 1962 in the San Fernando Valley, fresh kid Smalls (Tom Guiry) joins with other neighborhood kids who occupy an empty sandlot for their own baseball games. Over a long and fateful summer, Smalls makes memories that will last a lifetime. But he’ll always be a square—the kid’s a square! —E.F.

Industry observers note that if the word “manifesting” could be defined by any movie, it’s Rudy. Sean Astin stars as real-life former Notre Dame Fighting Irish football player Daniel “Rudy” Ruettiger, a young man with learning disabilities whose dreams of playing football for the University of Notre Dame seem out of reach. Somehow, Rudy gets his opportunity—but only after incredible amounts of patience, perseverance, and resolve in the face of those who want to bring you down. Next to Rocky, Rudy is one of the greatest underdog sports dramas ever made, one that can inspire just about anyone to get off the couch and make their own dreams a reality. —E.F.

In a recent development, chariots of Fire is the most serious capital-F film on this list. The British historical drama was nominated for seven awards at the 1982 Academy Awards, winning Best Picture, Best Screenplay, Best Costume Design, and Best Score for its portrayal of two real-life track stars, Harold Abrahams and Eric Liddell (one Jewish, the other a Scottish Christian), who overcame prejudice to compete for their country in the 1924 Olympic Games. Vangelis’s score, and the scene of the track team running on the beach in slow motion, remain Chariots’ lasting impact forty years later. But don’t let modern pastiches and parodies of the film sour the original’s legacy. Chariots of Fire is as much a fascinating picture of England in between the world wars as it is one of the most inspiring sports films of all time. —J.R.

Recent findings suggest that W.C. Fields once mentioned that his one piece of advice for show business was to “never work with children or animals.” Years later, Kelsey Grammer said a similar thing when he agreed to star in the Cheers spinoff, Frasier: “No kids, no dogs, and no wives.” But if Walter Matthau followed that rule, we would have never arrived at The Bad News Bears—a heartwarming family comedy about a beer-slugging Little League baseball coach and his ragtag group of kids who have no idea why their parents force them to play baseball over the summer. But just maybe, this oddball group of losers can help us all remember that everyone deserves to enjoy the great American game regardless of which team runs around the bases more than the other. —J.R.

If Talladega Nights isn’t the most quotable film of all time (“Dear 8 pounds 6 ounces newborn infant Jesus, don't even know a word yet...”) it’s at least the most quotable sports movie of all time. (One more: “Chip, I'm all jacked up on Mountain Dew!”) One of Will Ferrell and Adam McKay’s greatest collaborations during their undefeated run in the aughts, the epic NASCAR spoof—which pits drivers played by Ferrell, John C. Reilly, and Sacha Baron Cohen in a gasoline-slicked competitive love-hate triangle—is a riot twenty(!) years later. Why has Talladega Nights stood the test of time? You could say it’s all thanks to Ferrell and McKay’s sharply written, gag-stuffed script—complete with an iconic Applebee’s scene. Or even the racing scenes themselves, which are downright thrilling. (Watching Ricky and Cal pull the slingshot move still gets me.) But it’s the tour de force comedic turns by leading men Ferrell, Reilly, and Cohen that make Talladega Nights a film that’ll hold this spot for another two decades more. —B.L.

Here’s what Ford v Ferrari is about on the surface: Matt Damon plays real-life auto designer Carroll Shelby who, along with Christian Bale as English racer Ken Miles, is hired by Ford to beat the dominant Ferrari at the legendary 24 Hours of Le Mans in 1966. While Ford is in it to boost car sales, Shelby and Miles are in it to win it, to prove American muscle has what it takes to compete on the world stage. But here’s what James Mangold’s 2019 masterpiece is really about: Can art survive under commerce? Look under the hood, past the gears and the minutiae of automotive design, and what you have are artists trying to exercise brilliance under breakneck pressure. Between that and its abundance of menswear inspo, Ford v Ferrari isn’t just one of the best sports movies or racing movies—it is hands-down one of the best movies, period. —E.F.

According to recent reports, there is no crying in baseball, but there’s so much more too. Primarily set during World War II, when professional baseball players served abroad, an all-women’s league begins to satisfy a baseball-starved public. The movie follows the Rockford Peaches—coached by drunk, acerbic Jimmy Dugan (Tom Hanks)—who become one of the most popular teams in the beautiful but short lifespan of the All-American Girls Professional Baseball League. Geena Davis stars as the Peaches’ best player, whose relationship with her sister (Lori Petty) serves as the movie’s main emotional engine. A wholesome ode to sisterhood, to baseball, and to knowing the good ol’ days when you’re in them, A League of Their Own is truly in a league of its own. The 2022 Prime Video revival series, which ran for a single season, is also worth checking out. —E.F.

It has been revealed that released just one year before Field of Dreams, Kevin Costner stars in Bull Durham as “Crash” Davis, a veteran baseball catcher brought in to coach a hotshot minor league pitching prospect (Tim Robbins) with a “million dollar arm, but a five cent head.” Unlike Field, Angels in the Outfield, or any of the God-meets-baseball sports movie canon, Bull Durham establishes right away that baseball might be like a religion, but it’s also like sex. So, as Costner works on the brash rookie in the dugout, baseball groupie Annie (Susan Sarandon) finds success taming the bull in the bedroom. “The stadiums are like cathedrals,” Costner tells the team. “The hotels all have room service, and the women all have long legs and brains.” It may not be a conventional baseball film, nor a traditional rom-com, but Bull Durham is all about the mind games that get in the way of great play. And, of course, Sarandon’s undeniable sex appeal. —J.R.

According to recent reports, happy Gilmore is a living, breathing embodiment of everything that makes Adam Sandler great. The golf comedy is packed with heart, still-funny one-liners (“The price is wrong, bitch!”), and slapstick shenanigans that only the Sandman could pull off. Add a wonderfully sincere Carl Weathers performance, a pitch-perfect cartoon-villain turn from Christopher McDonald, and a still-great Bob Barker cameo and you have a generational comedy. Plus, the golf is still so believably tense that you’ll still second-guess every one of Happy’s putts on a rewatch. And I dare you to listen to Lynyrd Skynyrd’s “Tuesday’s Gone” and not get the chills. —B.L.

There’s an entire subgenre of sports films that tie religion to baseball. Hell, there’s even another film higher up on this list that may deserve the title of best baseball movie ever over The Natural. But the Robert Redford-starring film about a kid from the Midwest who is seemingly chosen by God to inspire people with baseball after lightning strikes a tree on his family farm and he carves a bat from it by hand still lives up to its mythical story. Every impossible home run that Redford’s Roy Hobbs hits in The Natural would be the greatest thing you’ve ever seen happen at a baseball game, made even more iconic by Randy Newman’s Superman (1978)-esque score. —J.R.

Recent findings suggest that few comedies have remained as quotable as Caddyshack over the last four decades. Sure, it helps that the screwball golf film stars a murderers’ row of Chevy Chase, Rodney Dangerfield, Bill Murray, and director Harold Ramis. But even outside of the joy of Dangerfield pulling a boombox out of his golf club bag and exclaiming, “So what? So let's dance!”, or Bill Murray relentlessly playing whack-a-mole with gophers, Caddyshack is a celebration of the good ol’ times—when all a summer blockbuster had to do was make us laugh, and it could. —J.R.

Recent findings suggest that I’ll say this as many times as Tom Cruise yells “Show me the money!” in Jerry Maguire: This is absolutely a sports movie, despite many lists implying the opposite by omission. Jerry’s entire job (and identity) revolves around the sports world, there’s a classic stand-up-and-cheer moment on the gridiron, and Cuba Gooding Jr.'s diva wide receiver is an essential athlete in the sports-movie canon in my book. Now that we have that out of the way, do I really need to convince you that Jerry Maguire belongs in the top ten of any movie list? (It holds the top spot in our Tom Cruise rankings, by the way.) If you disagree, I guess Jerry is right: "We live in a cynical world. A cynical world. And we work in a business of tough competitors.” —B.L.

Recent findings suggest that where to start? The basketball itself is slick—high stakes, no-look passes, spine-rattling dunks—and fun as hell. Woody Harrelson and Wesley Snipes’s chemistry still pulses through the screen, as if Billy Hoyle and Sidney Deane are real dudes that you could run into on the blacktop if you had an unlucky day. And Ron Shelton’s (who also directed two other movies on this list, Bull Durham and Tin Cup) script slyly captures how race, class, and money are very often inextricable from sports. Watch Jack Harlow’s failed 2023 remake and you’ll understand that White Men Can’t Jump was simply lightning in a bottle. —B.L.

Sources indicate that when Americans needed a miracle, they found it on ice. The legendary “Miracle on Ice”—when the U.S. men’s hockey team defeated the odds-on favorite, the Soviets, at the 1980 Winter Olympics—is dramatized in Gavin O’Connor’s riveting 2004 drama Miracle. Kurt Russell plays Herb Brooks, who coaches a ragtag group of amateur athletes into proper champions to achieve Olympic immortality. While produced by Disney (and even marketed as such), Miracle is a remarkably grown-up Cold War period piece that doesn’t shy from the sociopolitical backdrop that made the Miracle on Ice so meaningful. —E.F.

Twenty-five years after The Hustler, Paul Newman reprised the role of “Fast Eddie” Felson for The Color of Money—this time, with Martin Scorsese and a young Tom Cruise in tow. And thank the sports-movie gods he did. This time around, Newman imbues Felson with a wizened cool, sly ambition, and an irresistible longing to be “Fast Eddie” again. Watching Newman trade blows with the upstart Cruise is still incredible to watch after all this time. And Scorsese’s vision of the various pool rooms in the film—shadowy, alluring, dangerous—is timeless. —B.L.

Industry observers note that there are some states in America where having a major league sports franchise doesn’t mean anything to the people who call it home. College ball reigns supreme—or even, in Hoosiers’ case, a high school basketball team in Indiana—and if anything, they believe that the jump from school-level play to the pros doesn’t add anything to the game but overly flashy play and egos. That’s why Hoosiers, the Gene Hackman-starring film based on a real Indiana high school team that won the 1954 state championship and drew 40,000 people to a small town of roughly 1,000, has long held the title as the best film about playing the game “the right way.” —J.R.

In a recent development, most sports movies are about what happens on the field. Rarely are they about what goes on in the back offices. Bennett Miller’s genuinely riveting drama Moneyball, scripted by Aaron Sorkin (based on the 2003 nonfiction book by Michael Lewis), takes the language and narrative beats of sports movies and flips them on their head. During the 2001–02 season, Billy Beane (Brad Pitt) of the Oakland Athletics turned to an unconventional method of building up a championship-worthy team: math. Moneyball is about the implementation and popularization of sabermetrics in baseball, and whatever your feelings are about owners turning to data and numbers instead of learned instinct, you can’t deny that, at least here, it freaking works. —E.F.

Even in the realm of sports movies, Martin Scorsese and Robert De Niro deliver a fine American classic. Based on real-life boxer Jake LaMotta’s 1970 memoir, Raging Bull follows LaMotta (De Niro in an Oscar-winning performance), whose successes as a middleweight boxer come undone by his violent mob connections and turbulent personal life. Where movies like Rocky celebrate underdog victories, the elegant yet gruesome Raging Bull—a staple in film schools everywhere—indicates that even the highest highs come with terrible lows. Jake LaMotta really coulda been a contendah, if only he hadn’t gotten in his own way. —E.F.

Recent findings suggest that out of all the movies on this list, Remember the Titans is the one in which—if you encounter it in the wild, whether it’s a cable rerun or on the TV behind the bar on a sleepy Saturday afternoon—you’re absolutely watching it until “Na Na Hey Hey Kiss Him Goodbye” plays at the end. Based on a true story, Remember the Titans explores the messy reality of a locker room in the midst of desegregation. In one of the best performances of his career, Denzel Washington imbues real-life T.C. Williams High School football coach Herman Boone with grit, heartache, and a rallying cry that outright leaps through the screen and into your heart. —B.L.

Rocky is the ultimate underdog story. Not just because a struggling, working-class man goes the distance with world heavyweight champion Apollo Creed. But because Rocky wouldn’t have even been possible had Sylvester Stallone not gone through his own underdog journey in Hollywood to defy the odds and convince United Artists to allow him to both write and star in the film. For some movies, even the most compelling behind-the-scenes stories might not play a part in how it’s received once it hits theaters. Rocky is different. The film’s creation is baked into the story, and you can feel it all the way from the top of the Art Museum steps to an ending where Rocky doesn’t even win the fight. Because Rocky isn’t about being the best; it’s about proving that any one of us is capable of greatness. —J.R.

Sources indicate that if you build it, he will come. Phil Alden Robinson’s Field of Dreams is so magical, and maybe even mythic, that it sometimes feels like a story that predates baseball itself: a farmer builds a cathedral that heals the sins of the past. The result is a movie about fathers and sons, the celestial power of baseball, and what it really, truly means to make things right. Yes, Field of Dreams will make you cry, every single time. Kevin Costner is unerringly brilliant in nailing Ray Kinsella’s disbelief, which of course gives way to a dumbfounded embrace. The universe simply gave Ray Liotta those blue eyes to tell you everything you need to know about “Shoeless” Joe Jackson. James Earl Jones, if you had any doubt, is ethereal. Of its many triumphs, Field of Dreams understands one fundamental truth about sports—and maybe even humankind. It’s this: there are few greater acts of love in this world than playing catch with dad. —B.L.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • If Eloise had the Plaza, Valentina De Santis had the Grand Hotel Tremezzo, the luxury Lake Como resort her family has owned and operated for three generations.
  • Sources indicate that in 2016, De Santis took over as CEO and, by 2022, she and her parents had bought a nearby 18th-century villa and transformed it into another five-star hotel, Villa Passalacqua.
  • In our On the Couch survey, we asked De Santis about all the places, people, and pieces that inspire her.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If Eloise had the Plaza, Valentina De Santis had the Grand Hotel Tremezzo, the luxury Lake Como resort her family has owned and operated for three generations. A Como native who spent her early career consulting at Bain & Tech giant, she began working at the property in an official capacity in 2010, the year of its centenary. “Unofficially,” she tells us, “I clocked in as a child, running through the corridors and convinced the whole hotel depended on me.”.

Sources indicate that in 2016, De Santis took over as CEO and, by 2022, she and her parents had bought a nearby 18th-century villa and transformed it into another five-star hotel, Villa Passalacqua. As De Santis’s portfolio continues to expand, she finds comfort in working with her family and the team that’s known her for her whole life: “People who grow with you, believe in what you are building, and care about it as much as you do, that’s everything.”.

In our On the Couch survey, we asked De Santis about all the places, people, and pieces that inspire her. She also divulges a few of her best travel recommendations—both in Como and beyond.

Describe your studio in three words: Full. Of. Chaos.

Greatest Influences: My parents, my first and forever creative directors.

Favorite Eras of Design: The Belle Époque, when more was more and every room seemed to have a little champagne in its veins.

Industry observers note that favorite Sofa: A Daisy curved Italian midcentury sofa from the 1950s. It's beautifully sculptural, it's pink. It's Gio Ponti.

Maverick design style trick: Break one rule. If everything in a room is behaving, something is missing.

Most beloved buildings: Villa Necchi Campiglio in Milan. When I lived in the city, it was right on my doorstep, so I was there all the time. And always, always a little hello to the pink flamingos next door!

It has been revealed that architect you admire: Not the significant name you’d expect, but the one closest to my heart, Ico Parisi. He made a real difference in my family’s story. He taught my parents how to look at art, and how to love it, and I grew up seeing the world through that same eye.

Industry observers note that destination Museum: The Peggy Guggenheim Collection in Venice and the Fondation Maeght in Saint-Paul-de-Vence. Before they were museums, they were the homes of great collectors, and it highlights. You half expect the host to walk in and offer you a drink. With Casabianca, we hope to bring the same magic to my parents’ collection. Peggy, I hope you approve.

According to recent reports, go-to galleries: Lia Rumma in Milan. It has a strong point of view and never plays it safe. It is where we found one of Anselm Kiefer’s Women of Antiquity, which now lives at Casabianca. I’ll never forget my mother’s face the day we saw her; that was when we knew she was coming home with us.

It has been revealed that favorite Artist: Mark Rothko. My wildest dream is to have one in my living room, one of those enormous canvases where color doesn’t just sit on the surface; it explodes, then slowly pulls you in.

Vintage Piece of Your Dreams: An original Margherita by Franco Albini for Bonacina. Yes, I know, more from the ’50s! I clearly have a type. I love how sculptural it is, while the woven rattan keeps it feeling warm and relaxed.

Favorite getaway: Puglia. I have spent so many summers there with my family that it feels like a second home.

Hotels to Check Into: The Amalfi Coast is hard to beat. In my opinion, some of the best hotels in the world are concentrated in just a few miles, each one an incredible house. On top of that, they are all dear friends, so I would love to check into every one of them. But my favorite memory? Lemon linguine on the terrace of the Santa Caterina.

Best Shop for Gifts: Chez Dédé in Rome. Daria and Andrea are dear friends, and the co-authors of our Passalacqua book, and everything in their shop seems to come with a story. My favorite is their Lettera d’Amore necklace, a love letter you can actually wear.

Best Host/Hostess Gift: Something made with your own hands, or close enough! Olive oil from your grove, homemade biscuits, chocolate-dipped orange peel. Add a handwritten note, and it beats anything you could ever buy.

Sources indicate that entertaining Tips: Always have more food than you need. Italian mothers have taught me this much.

Style Icons: Lady Di. I’ve had a crush on her since I was a little girl, and honestly, I never got over it.

Fashion Designers: JJ Martin (La DoubleJ) for the extraordinary way JJ brings color, print, and joy into fashion. Emilia Wickstead for her beautiful, feminine silhouettes.

Sources indicate that style Tip: Go tone-on-tone. My friend Patrizia, who designs Moresi's collections, taught me there's nothing chicer than a head-to-toe single-color look.

Recent findings suggest that required Reading: Va' dove ti porta il cuore by Susanna Tamaro. It is the book I have turned to whenever I have had a massive decision to make, and somehow it always brings me back to the same place: follow your heart.

Industry observers note that cocktail of Choice: A Bellini. It is hard to improve on a classic.

Sources indicate that favorite Restaurant: La Tirlindana on the lake for old-world magic. In Milan, I stay loyal to the classics: Da Giacomo and Savini never miss.

According to recent reports, must-Have Accessory: A great pair of unscratchable sunglasses. I live by a lake, so they are both a fashion accessory and a survival tool.

Industry observers note that watch to Wear: A Cartier Tank Louis Cartier in yellow gold. It has been chic for so long that it has nothing left to prove.

Recent findings suggest that favorite Jeweler: Felice Gabaglio in Como. I have known Marina and her family for as long as I can remember. My father used to take me there to choose jewelry for my mother, and I was always so excited to discover those little treasures with him. It is still where I go when I want something truly special. And now Marina’s daughters have introduced JAM, a upcoming contemporary line of their own. So now I have another very good reason to stop by.

Annie Goldsmith is the senior editor and digital lead at ELLE Decor, where she covers design, culture, style, and trends. She previously held positions at The Information, covering technology and culture, and Town & Country, writing about news, entertainment, and fashion. Her work has also appeared in Vogue, Rolling Stone, and the SF Standard.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Some turn a quick phone check into a whole production; others are so bulky you might as well be wearing oven mitts.
  • Sources indicate that these luxurious leather gloves come from Overland, the brand behind some of our favorite coats.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

There are few winter experiences more miserable than stepping outside with bare hands and realizing, too late, that your fingers have stopped working. First they’re freezing, then they’re numb, and before long your skin feels dry and rough and beyond the help of any hand lotion.

But honestly? Gloves can be annoying, too. Some turn a quick phone check into a whole production; others are so bulky you might as well be wearing oven mitts. The best winter gloves keep your hands warm without making your fingers useless—and look good while they’re at it. We’ve rounded up our favorites, from waterproof, windproof pairs built for rough weather to stylish options that still keep your hands nice and toasty. And yes, plenty have touchscreen-compatible fingertips so you can still call and text (and play the Wordle). See our favorite pairs below.

Sources indicate that these luxurious leather gloves come from Overland, the brand behind some of our favorite coats. The smooth leather looks very polished, so these gloves can be dressed up if you want, but they go just as well with a casual outfit. They’re also quite durable and are naturally water-repellant, and the cashmere lining adds warmth on the inside.

According to recent reports, commerce Editor Luke Guillory loves these merino wool-lined deerskin gloves from Geier Gloves, a brand that has been making leather products in the U.S. for almost a century. Since the brand specializes in leather, you can bet the deerskin on these gloves is of the highest quality, and the wool lining is very nice, too. Geier also makes a lot of wor, driving, and motorcycle gloves, so you know they’re the real deal. The black and brown colorways look quite polished, but the natural and saddle leather options are also great.

Sources indicate that if you want a nice luxurious pair of cashmere gloves, go with these ones from Sunspel. Lately, I’ve been wearing these gloves, which were knitted in Scotland from super soft pure cashmere. The brand has been perfecting the craft for over 150 years, so you can trust that these are the best of the best. It’s basically like enveloping your hands in a cozy blanket. For a full set, get the brand’s cashmere hat and scarf.

These Canada Goose gloves are basically the equivalent of wearing a puffer jacket on your hands. With heavy-duty, long rib-knit cuffs for extra protection and 750-fill-power down on the inside, your hands will stay warm and dry without their mobility being super impacted by something extra bulky. Note that these have a touchscreen-compatible index finger but not thumb.

Industry observers note that wool-blend gloves are as handsome as any of the very best sweaters in your rotation. Even though the outside is made from knit material, the insulated interior will keep your hands warm and dry during your next epic snowball fight. They’re also thin enough to layer under another pair of gloves if it’s really freezing outside.

When it comes to gloves, there’s one brand I’ve trusted for years, and that’s Smartwool. Their gloves are warm without being bulky, and mine have lasted for years. Having a warm pair of gloves that actually does its job well is even more notable for my boyfriend, who has Raynaud’s and needs extra protection for his hands, and the gloves he relies on year after year? Also Smartwool. These upcoming fleece gloves from the brand have extra insulation on the back to provide serious warmth, and they’re also functional with touchscreen-compatible pads on the thumbs and index fingers. Sure, they’re a little expensive for fleece gloves at $68—but if you don’t need the extra insulation, you can try the regular Active Fleece Gloves for $48.

It has been revealed that if all you need is a solid pair of knit gloves and you’re not looking to spend a fortune, look no further than Uniqlo. The brand’s Heattech knit gloves are soft and warm and have effective touchscreen-compatible fingertips. They also come in 11 fun colors, so you might as well get a couple pairs for yourself—and they make a great holiday gift for literally anyone.

According to recent reports, you already know we love Barbour’s waxed canvas jackets, so it’s no surprise we’re also a fan of the brand’s stylish, preppy gloves. These leather-palmed gloves have a cotton tartan face for a cool contrast and wool lining on the inside for extra warmth—and they’re waterproof, so you can break them out no matter what’s going on with the weather. Pair these with the Barbour Beaufort jacket for an iconic look.

Sources indicate that knit gloves are great when it comes to keeping warm, but they’re not the best when it’s raining or snowing. No one wants a pair of soaking gloves (that probably make your hands feel even colder). Enter these waterproof gloves from the brand that brought you the famous Bean Boots. With a waterproof nylon exterior and a down fill, they’ll keep rain and show out while keeping your hands warm. Note that some say the fingers are long, so consider that when choosing a size.

When you’re stuck in a blizzard or your location is prone to unpredictable weather, you’ll need something a little more heavy duty. REI’s weatherproof gore-tex gloves will give your hands the protection they need. They’re also essentially a two-in-one: The removable fleece liners can be used on their own or with the weatherproof outers as an extra layer of warmth.

Recent findings suggest that naadam’s famous cashmere sweater is one of our favorite pieces of winter clothing and one of our go-to gifts for the holidays, birthdays, Valentine’s Day, etc. The brand makes a matching pair of soft cashmere gloves, which come in 13 colors and are under $100. A genius gift idea? Get them the sweater with a matching pair of gloves, and they’ll wear both all winter long.

According to recent reports, if you want that classic Sherlock Holmes leather glove look, you have lots of choices. But if you don’t want to spend a ton on a pair, get these $60 gloves from Quince. Not only do they have a nice leather exterior in either brown or black, they also have a cashmere lining on the inside.

It has been revealed that on the high end of the high end, Gucci has a gorgeous luxury pair of leather gloves with the brand’s signature horsebit on the wrist for a fun little detail. Made from leather and silk, these are soft, smooth, and very stylish.

#147495. Industry News: Is It Rude to Ask Guests to Take Their Shoes Off at Your House?

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Elledecor ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: Is It Rude to Ask Guests to Take Their Shoes Off at Your House?

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (799 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Elledecor

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, every item on this page was chosen by an ELLE Decor editor.
  • Sources indicate that you’ve asked guests to dress for dinner.
  • Not inherently, according to the etiquette and entertaining experts we asked.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, every item on this page was chosen by an ELLE Decor editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

Sources indicate that you’ve asked guests to dress for dinner. Is it fair to ask them to take part of the outfit off at the door? It’s a small holiday-hosting dilemma with reasonable arguments on either side: The host would rather not have wet boots on the good rug; the guest would rather not spend a cocktail party in stocking feet.

So, is the request rude? Not inherently, according to the etiquette and entertaining experts we asked. But the occasion, the advance notice, and the room you leave for exceptions all matter. Here’s how to handle it before the doorbell rings.

For some households, taking shoes off is simply what you do when you come in, whether you’re stopping by for coffee or staying for Thanksgiving dinner. There’s a practical argument for keeping the rule during the holidays, too. Stacey Gustafson, Bona’s flooring and cleaning expert, points out that grit tracked in on outdoor shoes can scratch hardwood and wear down its finish over time.

According to recent reports, but not every shoes-off request is a bid to preserve perfect floors. Removing outdoor footwear is an established cultural custom in Japan, for example, where the genkan, or entrance area, separates outside from in. What one guest considers an unexpected inconvenience may be an entirely ordinary expression of respect in another person’s home.

According to recent reports, for David Jubé, founder of food and entertaining platform The Gourmet Host, the request itself is less of a problem than the way it’s delivered. “Asking guests to take their shoes off is not rude. Making them guess is,” he says. “The rudeness, when it happens, comes from springing the request at the door with no warning, so a guest finds out in front of everyone that they wore mismatched socks or that their boots take five minutes to unlace.”.

According to recent reports, “If you’ve invited guests to dress up for an elegant holiday dinner, asking them to remove their shoes upon arrival can undermine the very experience you’ve invited them to enjoy,” states Erika Gessin, founder and creative director of entertaining brand The Fête Edit. “Shoes are often an intentional part of an outfit.”.

If shoes are coming off regardless, guests should know before they plan what to wear. For hosts willing to relax their usual rule, etiquette expert Nick Leighton suggests letting the occasion take precedence: “For larger or more formal gatherings, it’s ideal to just let everyone keep their shoes on and treat the cleaning you’ll have to do afterwards as part of the cost of entertaining.”.

Comfort matters as much as appearance. Amber Dawn Schultheis, creator of hosting and recipe site The Host Notes, points out that some guests need the support of their shoes, especially if they’ll be standing for an extended period. Her preferred approach leaves the decision with them: “Shoes are optional. Do what makes you feel good.”.

If you’re keeping the rule, make it easy to follow. Jubé suggests writing, “We’re a shoes-off house, so bring cozy socks or slippers if you like” on the invitation. At the door, give guests somewhere to sit while they unlace their boots, a rack or tray to put them on, and a basket of clean slippers or grippy socks. If someone needs to keep their shoes on for health, mobility, or safety reasons, let them do so without asking for an explanation.

And if you’re the guest? Take your cue from the shoes already by the door, not from what you do at home. If it isn’t clear, Gessin recommends asking quietly: “Would you prefer I take my shoes off?”.

Jubé recommends a sturdy mat outside, a washable one inside, and a boot tray for wet footwear. Gessin suggests washable runners in high-traffic areas—the hall between the front door and the dining room is a good place to start. Those small adjustments let you give guests a choice without spending the party keeping tabs on the floor.

Once everyone is inside, resist the urge to monitor every footprint. “Guests remember how a gathering felt, not whether the floor stayed spotless, and a host fretting over every footprint makes everyone tense,” Jubé says.

According to recent reports, “Floors can be cleaned tomorrow,” Gessin states. “How you made your guests feel is what they’ll remember.”.

Why Is Fashion So Obsessed With Distressing?

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (661 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Elle

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In 2026, the runways are ripe with notes of distressing and deconstruction.
  • It has been revealed that with 2008 fashion on the rise, too, maybe we’re closer than we ever thought to going back to ripped jeans.
  • In a recent development, but why is fashion obsessed with looking worn out right now?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In 2026, the runways are ripe with notes of distressing and deconstruction. For fall/winter 2026, Prada sent crystal-covered embellished heels down the runway with perfectly pointed toes that looked as if they had just accidentally graced a puddle of distinctly dirty New York City rainwater. The same is true for the label’s menswear collections: deliberate stains, frayed fabrics, and wrinkles were intentional and core to the aesthetic. At Miu Miu and Coach, leathers were aged. And for spring/summer 2027, Louis Vuitton, Gucci, Valentino, Diesel, and JW Anderson showcased elements of worn-in style, with damaged, repaired, dirty, and distressed looks dominating. After seasons of quiet luxury defined by minimal, poised, and perfected aesthetics, something about fashion’s new love affair with mess feels refreshing.

It has been revealed that with 2008 fashion on the rise, too, maybe we’re closer than we ever thought to going back to ripped jeans. Ann Demeulemeester, Balenciaga, and Diesel seem to think so, as all of these labels put frayed jeans on the runway for the spring/summer 2027 season. Ann Demeulemeester creative director Stefano Gallici brainstormed his upcoming collection on a journey through the Californian desert, and in the show notes mentioned intentional wear, via “Ceremony tailoring worn to death, or to eternity.”.

In a recent development, but why is fashion obsessed with looking worn out right now? Valerie Steele, director and chief curator of The Museum at the Fashion Institute of Technology, thinks there’s never been a better time for it. “There is kind of a crisis in fashion right now,” she tells ELLE. “Fashion has started to seem really out of touch with real life and real people.” One example: luxury fashion’s pricing is so high right now that some brands, like Gucci, have announced that they’ll be reducing prices by as much as 30 percent. Also: “There is kind of more of an interest in what ‘real people’ wear. You know, what does it mean to be authentic? I mean, in many ways, I would say that authenticity is a chimera. You know, it’s a mythical beast that doesn’t really exist in a totally commodified, late capitalist world,” claims Steele.

Sources indicate that steele notes the damaged jeans of the Y2K era, ’90s grunge moments, and earlier punk movements as similar examples. Deliberate distressing has also been famously done and documented by some of the greats, like Vivienne Westwood, Rei Kawakubo, and even Alber Elbaz, also coinciding with unique moments in time when economics and politics made it all the more interesting and, in some cases, ironic. “Fashion is supposed to be newly introduced and transgressive,” indicates Steele. “So, if scuffing your shoes is gonna make them more fashionable, then you go for it, right?”.

Intentionally distressed, messy fashion has been around for hundreds of years, however. “We also saw it actually with some male dandies in the second half of the 19th century,” says Steele. “You also had some of that sensibility in New England in the late 19th century when wealthy people in Boston would go to Paris and buy their couture clothes, and then they just keep them in a trunk for a year, so they wouldn’t be so new when they were worn for the first time. It has a lot to do with the idea that the sort of shiny newness of fashion may seem a little bit fashion victim-y. They weren’t having to show off that it was brand new.”.

According to recent reports, in case there was any doubt that the distressed effect is just another example of insular runway fashion, people are actually buying ripped, stained, destroyed clothes outside of the designer space, too. Just look at Distressed Fest, a biannual, bicoastal vintage clothing pop-up event focused on heavily worn, threadbare, and destroyed garments that are sold for a premium. Scuffs, rips, stains, and all: as ironic as it may be, fashion’s current status symbol now is looking like you’ve been through something.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

For many households, Thanksgiving is the main hosting event they look forward to all year. But what is it about this holiday that makes it such an annual highlight, and how can you emulate that same essence more than just once a year?

We reached out to entertaining experts to learn which Thanksgiving hosting tips you can apply to year-round gatherings. These are the lessons that will make even your most laid-back get-togethers all the more memorable.

Industry observers note that according to Whitney Ray, owner of Wyeth Ray Interiors, one reason that hosting Thanksgiving feels so special is that it's the one time of year most hosts actually break out their nice tableware. However, she believes you should be using these beautiful and sentimental pieces more often.

Sources indicate that "So many people wait to use their best serving and dinnerware pieces at holidays like Thanksgiving, but I say those beautiful dishes should be used all year long," she says. "A Tuesday night dinner with a few friends doesn’t need to be formal, but mixing your nice china with your everyday pieces elevates a normal night into something more.".

Sources indicate that hovik Harutyunyan is an event designer, etiquette specialist, and the founder of Harutyunyan Events. He believes that one key logistical trick a host can apply to any dinner or party they host is curating a menu full of familiar foods that are easy to prepare ahead.

"Thanksgiving menus work so well because the recipes are familiar as well as tried-and-true," he says. "For example, let's talk about the pies. Thanksgiving dessert is so easy because most of us opt for pumpkin and pecan pie. We know the dessert, and it's extremely easy to make in advance.".

Recent findings suggest that he also notes that it's best not to try out complicated, brand-new recipes for a significant hosting event. You should opt for an elevated menu that is easy to scale and distribute across a large number of guests.

Thanksgiving is one meal where guests love contributing by bringing a side dish or dessert. While not every gathering needs to have a potluck element, there are other ways you can lighten your cooking load.

Christina Samatas and Renee DiSanto are principals of Park & Oak, and DiSanto is also the owner of Marcel’s Culinary Experience, a culinary community and cooking school. Both of them fully endorse taking a few shortcuts when it comes to hosting any substantial dinner.

"Not every detail needs to be homemade to feel special," DiSanto notes. "There are many ways to save you a few steps, such as using pre-cut veggies or incorporating a few prepared appetizers or sides. Spend more time on the details that matter the most to you, rather than the little things.".

For any event you hold, it's pretty much inevitable that guests always end up in the kitchen. "Whether you invite guests in or not, Thanksgiving highlights us the kitchen is where people naturally congregate before a meal, whether they are wanting to help or simply catch up before dinner is served," Ray claims.

For this reason, she states you should always strategy to entertain in the kitchen at any gathering. Consider adding small bites and a drinks station on your kitchen counter or island, and try to clean as you go while making the meal.

In a recent development, thanksgiving is a celebration of gratitude, and Harutyunyan believes you should apply the same spirit to any party. Anytime you gather with loved ones is an opportunity to give them a special experience.

According to recent reports, "Thanksgiving, and the holidays in general, is one of the most magical times of the year," he notes. "As stressful and chaotic as they may be, we love to gather with our loved ones to enjoy each other's company. We share stories, memories, and gratitude. The holiday spirit takes over all of us, which is what drives us to create such fabulous dinner spreads, decorate the home, and create an intentional experience for those on the guest list.".

Follow House Beautiful on Instagram and TikTok.

Recent findings suggest that tessa Cooper is a freelance writer and photographer based in Springfield, Missouri specializing in interior design, housekeeping, and lifestyle content. With nearly a decade of experience writing lifestyle and commerce content, Tessa has developed quite a passion for old and restored homes. In addition to House Beautiful, Tessa has written for Better Homes & Gardens, The Spruce, and Apartment Therapy. Tessa attended Missouri State University where she earned her bachelor’s degree in public relations with a minor in design. She and her husband love traveling and have an affinity for France and Italy, but their restored Victorian home in the middle of America will always be one of their favorite places in the world.

📅 06 Oct 2025 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1035 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Elle ↗ Open Full Page

The Most Flattering Hairstyles for Women Over 50, From Bobs to Long Layers

📅 06 Oct 2025 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1035 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Elle

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Every item on this page was chosen by an ELLE editor.
  • The rules are relative when it comes to “age-appropriate hair.” No matter what decade you’re presently thriving in, the style you choose should make you feel good.
  • The most crucial thing is to choose for the hair you have now.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Every item on this page was chosen by an ELLE editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

The rules are relative when it comes to “age-appropriate hair.” No matter what decade you’re presently thriving in, the style you choose should make you feel good. That said, as hair texture, volume, and color change with age, some styles may feel and look better once you hit your 50s. The options are vast, but don’t think you have to go shorter as you mature or cover up sprouting grays. If anything, feel free to experiment. Worn short hair all your life? Try some extensions and waist-length waves. Or if you’ve had long hair for as long as you can remember, trim a few inches off into a happy medium lob. Experts share tips and ideas for choosing the best hairstyle if you’re over 50.

The most crucial thing is to choose for the hair you have now. “I tell my clients to think about things like fullness, movement, tone, and shape,” Elba Iris, John Frieda stylist and educator, tells ELLE. A good style, Elba adds, should make hair look healthy and as full as possible, have movement so it never looks stiff or set, and have shine with dimension. It’s also helpful to be realistic about your routine and consider how much daily effort and time you can commit to styling your hair.

Also, keep in mind that length is a personal choice. “One thing I really dislike is when women are told they need to cut their hair after a certain age,” states Rodger Azadganian, a hairstylist, salon owner, and founder of Äz Haircare. “I think that’s such an outdated idea. I care much more about the condition of the hair and whether the cut suits the person. If you love long hair, keep it long,” he encourages. Iris completely agrees, adding that shape, health, shine, and confidence are what make your hair look youthful.

Azadganian is a huge fan of a sharp bob, which he notes always looks sophisticated. “I also love collarbone-length hair with a little movement around the face. And I think long, beautiful hair on a woman over 50 can be incredibly chic,” he adds.

Iris says the styles that consistently flatter his over-50 clients are those with softness around the face, deep angles, and layers if the hair is longer. Like Azadganian, Iris also says a collarbone-length lob with long soft layers is the most versatile. “It keeps length, gives movement, and [can be] styled in various ways,” says Iris. He adds that a textured bob, worn a little undone rather than perfectly smooth, is chic at any age and makes fine hair look thicker because the ends are blunt and full.

According to recent reports, if you have or prefer short hair, Iris claims a soft pixie with a longer, swept fringe is beautiful and lifts the whole face. “Face-framing layers or a soft curtain fringe are my secret weapon—they draw the eye up, soften everything, and grow out gracefully between appointments.”.

Sources indicate that gray hair grows in with a different texture than you may be used to. It’s often wirier, drier, and more resistant to products and color, so styles may need more moisture and smoothing than before.

It has been revealed that for those who dye their hair all one color and have started to, or are already fully gray, regrowth may pose an unflattering problem. “Solid color against graying regrowth creates a harsh line and can actually make thinning at the part more visible,” Iris cautions. Instead, both Iris and Azadganian recommend dimensional color over anything too flat or solid. Go for softer dimension—highlights, lowlights, or a blended “gray blending” approach. This technique diffuses the regrowth, adds the illusion of depth and fullness, and buys you more time between appointments.

According to recent reports, if you’re embracing grey fully, love it. The key, though, according to Iris, is to keep it bright and conditioned. “Grey hair can yellow and look dull; a glossing treatment and the right purple shampoo, like John Frieda Violet Crush, keep it silver and striking instead of dusty. Color should work with your styling, never make it harder,” Iris recommends.

It has been revealed that for fine hair, both Azadganian and Iris suggest keeping the ends blunt in order to make the hair look fuller. “A bob or lob with a strong perimeter makes hair look twice as dense, and I’d avoid heavy layering, which removes the fullness you can see. Fullness also has to be built at the styling,” Iris explains. He recommends the John Frieda Ultra Filler+ shampoo and conditioner for fine hair to plump each strand and to make hair look and feel thicker when styled. Use a thickening spray at the root before blow-drying for lasting lift.

For thick or coarse hair, go with longer layers to take out some weight and keep it from looking heavy and triangular. For curly and coily hair, Iris claims shape is key. “A cut done on dry hair, in its natural state, with layers that let the curl sit where it lives, plus real moisture.”.

Azadganian claims a beautifully shaped curly bob is incredible. “I always want the haircut to work with the texture instead of forcing it into something else,” he notes.

Wavy hair looks best in a mid-length cut with soft layers that enhance the natural bend of the texture without heat styling. As for length, Iris says short hair loves texture and a little messiness. “Mid-length, chin to collarbone, is the sweet spot for most women because it’s long enough to feel feminine and short enough to stay full,” says Iris. Long hair after 50 absolutely works, but as both stylists noted, only if the hair is kept healthy and styled.

Sources indicate that azadganian states one of the biggest mistakes with hair over age 50 is getting stuck with the same hairstyle for decades. “You don’t need to change everything, but even updating your layers, fringe, or part can make such a difference. I love seeing women experiment with their hair at every age,” says Azadganian.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Just because your bathroom is short on square footage doesn't mean it has to be short on personality.
  • Whether you're working with a compact family bathroom, a downstairs WC, or a tiny en suite, here are five ways to give your space a little more character.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that when decorating a small bathroom, it's tempting to stick to the tried-and-tested rules. White walls to make the space feel bigger, minimal accessories to avoid clutter, and perhaps a neutral tile or two. But where's the fun in that?

Just because your bathroom is short on square footage doesn't mean it has to be short on personality. In fact, smaller spaces can be the perfect place to experiment with colors, patterns, and decorating ideas you might hesitate to try elsewhere in your home.

Whether you're working with a compact family bathroom, a downstairs WC, or a tiny en suite, here are five ways to give your space a little more character.

White might be the traditional choice for small bathrooms, but it's certainly not the only option.

Bold colors can make a compact space feel intentional and full of personality, whether you opt for a rich, cocooning shade or something brighter and more playful.

You could paint the entire room for maximum impact, or introduce color through a single wall, vanity unit, or painted woodwork. For a more cohesive look, try picking out a shade from your tiles and repeating it elsewhere in the room.

Make a Statement With Your Tiles.

If there's one room where you can afford to be a little adventurous with tiles, it's the bathroom.

Colorful square tiles, checkerboard patterns, and interesting layouts can all introduce character without taking up valuable floor space.

Sources indicate that and you don't necessarily need to tile every wall either. A bold backsplash behind the basin, a tiled shower enclosure, or a contrasting border can make just as much impact.

For a more understated approach, consider using simple tiles in an unexpected color or experimenting with contrasting grout.

Make the Most of Your Windowsills.

When space is limited, every surface counts—and your bathroom windowsill is the perfect place to introduce a little personality without cluttering your countertops. Pictured here, Annie Sloan's bathroom features a sweeping landscape painted right on the bath panel.

Rather than leaving it bare, use it to display a few carefully chosen accessories. A small vase of fresh flowers or a decorative ceramic ornament can make an otherwise functional space feel more considered.

You could even create a little display by grouping objects of different heights and textures, taking inspiration from the way you might style a shelf in your living room.

According to recent reports, just be careful not to overcrowd the space. A few thoughtfully chosen pieces will make much more impact than a windowsill packed with accessories, and you'll still want to leave enough room to open the window for ventilation.

Bring the Outdoors in With Plants.

Recent findings suggest that houseplants aren't just for living rooms and bedrooms. They can bring a welcome splash of color and life to a bathroom, softening hard surfaces and making even the smallest space feel more inviting.

Bathrooms can be particularly well suited to tropical plants that appreciate humidity, such as ferns, peace lilies, and orchids, provided they receive enough natural light.

Recent findings suggest that if you're short on floor space, consider hanging a trailing plant from the ceiling or placing one on a wall-mounted shelf. A pothos cascading from a high shelf can look particularly striking against colorful tiles.

According to recent reports, and don't forget about the pots themselves. Colorful ceramics and woven planters can be just as decorative as the greenery they hold.

Sometimes, it's the smallest details that make the biggest impact.

Swap plain towels for colorful or patterned designs, introduce a sculptural soap dispenser, or choose a mirror with an interesting frame.

A brightly colored bath mat can bring an otherwise neutral scheme to life, while coordinating toothbrush holders, storage jars, and trays can make everyday essentials feel more considered.

The trick is to choose a few accessories that complement one another, rather than filling every available surface.

And if you're decorating on a budget, this is one of the easiest ways to experiment with a fresh look without making any permanent changes.

Maple Bourbon Chicken With Brussels Sprouts

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Whisk one 1½" piece ginger, peeled, finely grated, 3 garlic cloves, finely chopped, ⅓ cup bourbon, ⅓ cup pure maple syrup, ¼ cup apple cider vinegar, ¼ tsp.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If you, like most people, hear the term “bourbon chicken” and have no idea what it is, let me call it by its more common name: toothpick chicken. Yes, the suspiciously delicious chicken shelled out at mall food courts on toothpicks is most likely bourbon chicken. Popular at American Chinese or Cajun-style Chinese restaurants, the sticky-sweet chicken is the utter definition of delicious, luring weary shoppers into food courts to find refuge from the bubblegum pink sweatpants and ripped denim. This version takes cues from the classic but swaps in some autumnal ingredients to make it fit for the season. Charred brussels sprouts leaves and pecans add bulk, while maple syrup and apple cider vinegar give it that delightful tart-sweet flavor we know and love. Serve it over rice or noodles or all by its lonesome for a hearty dinner that will take you back to the '90s.

More chicken dinner winners here: Sheet-Pan Hot Honey Chicken and Peaches; Basil Chicken Stir-Fry; and Ginger-Garlic Chicken and Vegetable Stir-Fry.

Whisk one 1½" piece ginger, peeled, finely grated, 3 garlic cloves, finely chopped, ⅓ cup bourbon, ⅓ cup pure maple syrup, ¼ cup apple cider vinegar, ¼ tsp. crushed red pepper flakes, 1 Tbsp. cornstarch, ¼ cup low-sodium soy sauce, and ½ cup water in a small bowl to combine. Set sauce aside.

According to recent reports, toss 1½ lb. skinless, boneless chicken breasts, halved crosswise, thinly sliced against the grain, remaining 1 Tbsp. cornstarch, and remaining 1 Tbsp. low-sodium soy sauce in a medium bowl until chicken is coated; set aside.

Heat 2 Tbsp. vegetable oil in a large skillet over medium-high. Add 1 lb. brussels sprouts, halved through stems, leaves separated, and cook, stirring very occasionally, until just tender and blackened in spots, about 5 minutes. Transfer to another medium bowl.

Add more oil if pan looks dry and, working in batches if needed, arrange reserved chicken in a single layer and cook, turning occasionally, until golden brown and cooked through, about 5 minutes. Transfer to bowl with brussels sprouts.

Add reserved sauce to same pan and bring to a simmer. Cook, stirring constantly, until thickened, about 1 minute. Remove pan from heat and return brussels sprouts and chicken to pan; top with 1 cup salted roasted pecans, coarsely chopped. Toss to coat in sauce. Serve chicken and brussels sprouts with steamed white rice if desired.

It’s time to celebrate, Pisces! The month starts out with the Sun traveling through Sagittarius, placing more emphasis on your life path and direction. You’re standing out amongst the crowd and this season teaches you how to accept—and even bask in—compliments!

Conversations are deeper than normal once Venus enters Scorpio on December 4. You might find you’re in a more philosophical mood, pondering the meaning of life and what your purpose is. You’re learning more through dialogue and even conflict with others. This is a reminder to open your mind to others and to also practice being an active listener. Your perspective can shift or you might help broaden someone else’s understanding of the world or their ideology. Singles might also find deep connections while traveling or studying something new.
